Table 4: Levels of schooling in Rwanda (Source: Ministry of Education, 2018 Education Statistics)

The equal rates of primary education for boys and girls in Rwanda suggests a cultural value of education for all children, not only prioritization for boys. A lack of tuition fees for childhood education enables poor families to send boys and girls to school, and increasing rates of education contributes to falling illiteracy rates in Rwanda (IUCN, 2021). Higher levels of girls in secondary education may be attributed to Rwanda’s national policy on gender equality and the government’s support for a free secondary head teacher program (IUCN, 2021). Despite lower rates of women enrolled in tertiary education, the percentage is increasing due to flexible programming such as online learning or night school, which enables women with family responsibilities to continue their studies. However, because of the low levels of education that women and men receive, the less likely they are to work in the agriculture sector (IUCN, 2021). 92% of women with no education work in agriculture (IUCN, 2021).

Strong gender stereotypes in Rwanda still push girls into traditionally “soft” trades including hairdressing, secretarial and nursing. Women are less likely to pursue a university degree work in the service sector (IUCN, 2021). Though women are more likely to be primary school teachers than men, they are rarely secondary, tertiary or technical/vocational teachers. In agriculture, women predominantly occupy informal positions such as weeding and harvesting crops while men hold more formal positions and higher ranging positions or manage higher value products such as timber (IUCN, 2021). As a result, the majority of agroforesters are male in Rwanda (Anastase & Nähnyi, 2020).

One of the greatest challenges to achieving economic stability lies in challenges in achieving quality education for all children. This is particularly true among girls and women with lower literacy, especially in rural areas. Overall, social factors including traditional gender roles such as domestic chores and family care; historic marginalization of girls and women, patriarchal social traditions, and gender-based violence entrench girls’ and women’s exclusion from educational opportunities (UNICEF, 2019). The lack of girls in the primary leaving exam results in girls being admitted to lower quality secondary schools, and ultimately into higher education institutions (HEIs) in lower numbers (Huggins & Randall, 2007).

This results in limited access to paid labor and employment in sectors such as agribusiness or public governance. Women are also underrepresented in the agricultural sector; commercialization of farming has made it more difficult to feed families. While there are national laws and policies to protect employment, there is little protection for the vast majority of women who work in informal sectors, significantly limiting their access to social security (IUCN, 2021). Women in rural areas are primarily care-providers for children and the elderly, which is unpaid labor and invisibilized due to gender norms (Abbot, 2015). Thus, understanding these barriers and challenges and how to overcome them will inform interventions at project-level.

### Patterns of power and decision-making

Rwanda is internationally acclaimed for being the first nation to have a majority female Parliament, with 61% in the 2013 election and 74.5% in the 2022 (Republic of Rwanda, 2019). The Constitution of the Republic of Rwanda established a minimum of 30% female representation in public governance, and this high level of female participation in upper levels of government far exceeds this minimum (East African Community, 2009). However, female participation drastically decreases in many communities

### Figure 7: Female and male representation in different levels of local government in Rwanda in 2018-2019 (Republic of Rwanda, 2019)

Although overall female representation in the Rwandan government is increasing, higher levels of female representation in upper levels of governance mirror the disparity between gender equality policy and practice in the country. In higher levels of governance, these policies are implemented well and appear effective. However, at lower levels of governance, there remains a significant gap between desirable gender gaps exist in central government roles that undergo recruitment processes, with many of these positions not reaching the 30% female representation minimum (Republic of Rwanda, 2019). Female representation within the police force is extremely low, although representation is high in most other areas of the sector just.

Similarly, in the private sector, women hold very few high level positions, particularly at the provincial levels. Women are more likely to be found in lower-level positions, but they do hold important positions at the provincial level (Republic of Rwanda, 2019). Women have high levels of representation in second vice presidency in the private sector, with 70% of national and 80% of provincial second vice presidential roles being held by women. However, this is not reflected in other senior leadership or executive positions (Republic of Rwanda, 2019). In more local organizations, such as cooperatives, men hold the majority of decision-making positions, while women tend to hold stereotypically female roles, such as record keeping and bookkeeping.

At the household level, women have very little decision-making power. Although under the 1999 Inheritance and Marital Property Law women are legally allowed to own land, cultural barriers still inhibit men from sharing this information with their wives or daughters. The law states that men are the head of the household, and thus are the primary owners of all of the family’s land and assets (IUCN, 2021). Women's lack of power within their households limits their ability to make decisions about the purchase of goods and services for the household as well as their ability to participate in income-generating activities. Based on female reports, the majority of households (70%) make decisions jointly, while in 25% of households the husband makes the majority of the decisions

# Gender equality and empowerment

## Service and support systems that contribute to gender empowerment, wellbeing, and security

Government mandated and running social service programs have reduced the percentage of extremely poor households from 23% and 26% in 2010 to 15% and 18% in 2017 for Mihits and Frits respectively. Three major social service support programs have contributed significantly to these observed reductions in poverty and increasing wellbeing and security.

The Ginkira Program (One Cow per Family Program) of the Ministry of Agriculture (MINAGIRI) started in 2006. By 2017 over 290,000 cows have been provided to vulnerable male and female headed households. The program aims at increasing household income through milk sales, increase the productivity of agricultural labor, generate a new stream of income through surplus milk sales and strengthen social cohesion amongst Rwandan families and communities as cow owners pass on surplus calves to other family members.

The largest social support program of the Government of Rwanda is the Vision 2020 Urumeenge Programme (VUP) which was started in 2008 and is managed by the Local Administrative Entities Development Unit (LEDU). The VUP has four components: wage labor through public works, direct cash transfers, financial services and awareness raising. The majority of public works support agricultural production, land conservation and the reclamation of degraded lands. Women are more likely to be employed in public works than men who are often captured by farming. Retaining control over VUP income was easier for women who owned an individual savings account (e.g., within a Savings and Credit Cooperative - SACCO), though most women did not have access to such accounts.

The financial services component of the VUP aimed at increasing access to credit, but women were more disempowered than men through cultural constraints to speaking in public meetings, workloads that limited participation in community meetings and self-help associations, and limited access to credit and savings. Women who had access to a VUP SACCO account were more likely to report that they were unaware of the existence of a VUP GRM, or were skeptical about the effectiveness of this complaint process. The most important recommendations were to a) enable women to open their own formal bank accounts to increase their control over their incomes and strengthen their decision-making capacity, and

### CONCLUSIONS: ONGOING CHALLENGES TO GENDER EQUITY IN THE CONTEXT OF THE ICRFV PROJECT

Despite tremendous efforts from the policy and legal perspectives, a patriarchal culture and persistent disparities in access to resources continue to impede women’s ability to participate fully in education; primary education; to access and control of property including land and economic resources; in employment opportunities and entrepreneurship; in decision-making at household and community levels; in family planning services; and in the provision of adequate sexual and reproductive health care, protection, and insecurity. Sexual and gender-based violence persists at high levels in Rwanda. While women have made impressive political progress, especially at the national level, their progress in terms of local political participation and engagement remains unequal. Economic opportunities remain markedly gender-differentiated.

In Rwanda and in the Congo-Nile Divide, structural barriers to economic and political equity and female empowerment have significantly impeded measures to adapt to climate change impacts. In Rwanda, structural barriers include women’s limited access to land, credit, and other resources; the results of leading gender-considerate policies across sectors. However, the point remains that women's ability to access, use and control natural resources, infrastructure and services differently is still low compared to men. This means that climate change will have a greater impact on women’s livelihoods than it does for men differently, and will generally result in greater vulnerability of women. Women are vital agents of change and can be powerful leaders from the community to global level in mitigating and adapting to climate change.

### 1.14 Afforestation, agroforestry and tree tenure

Kiptot et al (2012) noted that an ICRFV survey conducted across countries in eastern Africa concluded that women rarely have tenure over trees unless they exclusively have tenure over the land. Moreover, they stated that “women are more likely to be involved with fruit trees than timber trees and tend to have little or no commercial value. These products are mainly indigenous fruits...foodder and mulch.” They also noted that: "the survivorship of trees and fodder shrubs planted by men and women was effectively the same, but the economic benefits were significantly greater for those trees and shrubs relative to women farmers given that they are both labor and capital limited. Fuelwood, fodder, green manure, and enhancing crop production substantially increases benefits to women that cannot be captured by men." Women’s access to tree tenure is also important because it provides them with food (e.g., fruits, fodder, poles) and sell the surplus in local markets. It is unclear whether women who sell wood products from land that is owned by their husbands are able to capture that revenue stream.

Agroforestry offers multiple benefits to Rwandan farmers, in particular, women. Planting trees within agricultural fields can increase yields of crops, improve soil fertility and resilience of communities; agroforestry practices sequester carbon, prevent erosion, and enhance soil quality for sustainable

# 1.15 Improved cook stoves

In rural areas of Rwanda, 80% of households rely on wood as their main cooking fuel. The GoF completed a comprehensive report on Gender in the Energy Sector. The report noted that almost 60% of FHMs spend more than one day collecting firewood compared to 39% of MfHs. The latter purchased fuelwood twice as often as FHMs who primarily rely on gathering fuelwood. Over 50% of both Rwandan FHMs and MfHs still cook using the three-stone method, and only 13.5% use efficient cookstoves. Over half (54%) of all women in Rwanda are estimated to be exposed to smoke from cooking fires, which is linked to higher rates of respiratory disease. The report noted that women are more likely than men to be responsible for collecting firewood and were less likely to be involved in decision-making about fuel use. The report also addressed the fact that in higher altitude areas cooking with wood can lead to health problems due to smoke inhalation, which is linked to increased respiratory diseases.

### 1.16 Honey production and marketing

The Rwandan government has identified beekeeping as a potential source of additional revenue for farmers, particularly women who are often excluded from other agricultural activities (Mushonga et al., 2019). Beekeepers have been trained in Rwanda, indicating a market incentive to raise bees beyond subsistence level (Mushonga et al., 2019). Furthermore, global decline of bee populations reflects a high biological need for more apiarists in Rwanda. The Rwandan government has identified beekeeping as an important activity and is promoting it as a vocation for poor people. Out of 83,000 beekeepers in Rwanda, 86% are adult males and 71% lack primary education (Mushonga et al., 2019). To overcome the negative stigma around beekeeping, the government has launched a campaign to promote beekeeping as an important activity. Modern hives produce a higher yield of honey, have lower risk of causing fires, and do not need to be placed as high up in trees as traditional hives, which deters some women due to cultural restrictions barring women from climbing trees (Mushonga et al., 2019). Beekeeping is also promoted by the World Wildlife Fund, Philos, demonstrating a need for more modern tools (WCS, 2018). Additionally, marketing training may help women to better sell the honey, as women still have relatively low market and distribution access in Rwanda. Despite the stigma, beekeeping remains a strong potential source of income, which could reduce rural poverty levels (Mushonga et al., 2019; Mushonga et al., 2018; Mushonga et al., 2010).

A study by Mushonga (2019) suggests that people consider beekeeping for the poor and illiterate are largely the domain of older men no longer able to labor in agricultural production. Women do appear to be engaged in the production and marketing of honey bee. ADF provided $34,500 in 2017 to strengthen the honey production sector in Rwanda. Production remains relatively low because of disease, lack of access to markets, and poor infrastructure (Mushonga et al., 2019). The CDDIT (2009). The CDDIT report funded by the SNV noted that for 2009, of the estimated 30,293 beekeepers in Rwanda only 23% were women. The report recommended that the GoR do away with subsidies to beekeepers and instead provide training and credit to individual apiaries. This recommendation seems not the effects, encouraging beekeepers to actively participate in their own development and advocating for the replication of knowledge and skills from common to individual apiaries.

During focus groups both women and marginalized groups noted that the cost of modern hives and other beehive equipment such as smokers was a barrier to entry as was lack of access to credit. A big concern was farmers' use of pesticides that kill bees, making it impossible to locate apiaries near farmland.


### 1.17 Coronavirus (COVID-19) implications in advancing gender equity

The global coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic left no country untouched from its impacts. While research is still emerging, the severity of the pandemic is clear: strunging economies, vast unemployment, and threats to health and wellbeing continue to affect the global community. Women in particular are already


---
**Page 200**
---

vulnerable to socioeconomic inequality that is currently exacerbated by COVID-19. Therefore, the impact of the pandemic must be considered in gender planning into the future.

Ratcliffe and Hutchinson (2020) compared the secondary impacts of COVID-19 to the Ebola crisis on women and girls in Africa, finding that women and girls are more likely to experience higher poverty and financial empowerment, school dropouts, an increase in unintended pregnancies, reduced income and financial empowerment, increased rates of gender-based violence, and food insecurity due to the pandemic. In times of crisis, school closures and financial stress also lead to increased rates of gender based violence (Ratcliffe & Hutchinson, 2020). Women face greater exposure to COVID-19 in their homes because they are more likely to be caregivers for children and have less decision-making power, rendering their needs unmet during COVID (Perry & Gorter, 2020). In response, some countries have enacted policies to address the gendered impacts of the pandemic.

In Rwanda, the Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion (MIGEFP), in partnership with UN WOMEN and other partners, launched a rapid assessment on the impact of COVID-19. The report indicates that 44.2% of female respondents completely stopped their economic activities due to the pandemic, compared to only 17% of men (Bayisenge, Lo & Schreiner, 2020). In rural areas, the percentage was higher at 53%. Women also lost access to other sources of income, compared to 17.7% of rural men (Bayisenge, Lo & Schreiner, 2020). As women occupy more informal and unskilled jobs in Rwanda, they are at greater risk of income loss than men.

The use of health care and maternal services in Rwanda considerably declined during the COVID-19 outbreak. The decline was attributed to fear of contracting COVID-19 and lack of access to maternity vaccinations, which could be detrimental to avoiding future outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases (Wanyana, Wong & Hakimoto, 2020). Many women feared contracting the virus while attending health facilities, which contributed to the decline of health services in Rwanda (Wanyana, Wong & Hakimoto, 2020).

Recommendations to mitigate the impacts of COVID-19 on women in Rwanda include (Bayisenge, Lo & Schreiner, 2020):

- Implement programs that offer employment or financial security in spite of COVID-19.
- Provide online or socially-distant courses to prevent school dropouts.
- Establish woman-specific financial packages in the national economic recovery plan.
- Strengthen the mobilization of men and boys in childcare and domestic responsibilities to offset increased workload on women during the pandemic. Implement "Men engage" national programmes.
- Accelerate government interventions to address elevated levels of GBV.

### 1.18 Promoting gender equity within the CND GCF project

Gender equality and women's empowerment should be considered in all stages of the CND project cycle: design, formulation, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. In each of these stages, project managers should keep a 'gender lens' in mind, looking at ways the project can:

- Address gender inequalities that emerge from the project.
- Ensure the differential needs of women and men are addressed.
- Enhance access and participation for women in decision-making processes, services, and capacity development;
- Ensure equal participation of women and men in management arrangements and as


---
**Page 201**
---

beneficiaries, partners and key stakeholders; and
- Ensure women’s equal participation in decision-making processes.

Based on key expected outcomes, this gender assessment provides the foundation for a realistic gender action plan to be implemented in the CND project.

# GENDER, YOUTH AND SOCIAL INCLUSION ACTION PLAN

The goal of the programme is to increase climate resilience of vulnerable rural communities in the CND, reduce CO2 emissions, build capacity for integrated spatial planning and increase the extent and integrity of forest ecosystems in the CND. The programme has three components directly targeting vulnerabilities within climate impact chains: Component (1) Mainstreaming Climate Adaptation into Integrated Spatial Planning and Development; Component (2) Landscape Management and Restoration to Reduce Vulnerability to Climate Change; and Component (3) Enhancing Resilience of both ecosystems and rural populations, by strengthening coordination among sectors and integrating climate resilience considerations into planning and development. Component (2) Landscape Management and Restoration is designed to reduce vulnerability in the CND through landscape restoration and thereby increasing the extent and integrity of forest ecosystems and landscapes and by reducing demand for wood fuel. In addition, component (2) is designed to reduce the time women spend collecting and preparing firewood, which can be used as a proxy indicator of gender equality and improved decision making (see also Component 1). As a co-benefit, greenhouse gas emissions will be reduced through restoration of natural forests, agroforestry, reduced fuelwood demand and fuel efficient cookstoves under component (2) are expected. Component (3) will focus on Enhancing climate adaptation through resilient livelihoods.

Women, youth and marginalized groups, including women-headed households in the CND are key stakeholders in the success of this project, and are the primary target beneficiaries of the project. The emphasis is placed on increasing their resilience to climate change by strengthening communities around Nyungwe National Park and Gishwati-Mukura National Park-critical for Rwanda yet highly vulnerable forests due to high population and increasing demography who depend upon fuelwood, and actions taken by poor households that illegally use forests to improve income streams.

## 1.9 Methods

This Action Plan operationalizes the findings from the Gender Assessment, the EISA, and youth-based information collected during the feasibility studies and stakeholder engagement during the Project Preparation Facility (PPF) phase. The Assessment used five standard lenses (USAID 2017[3]) to conduct the analysis:

- Institutions, Laws and Policies that influence the context in which men and women act and make decisions.
- Beliefs, Perceptions, and Cultural Norms that shape how men and women, youth and elders are able (or expected) to participate actively, particularly those to be developed by this GCF project.
- Gendered Power Relations and Time Poverty that affect access to resources.
- Access to and Control over Assets and Resources are different between young and old, men and women.
- Patterns of Power and Decision-making focused on how individuals are able to be represented and be in decision-making positions.

Based upon this framework of five lenses, the Gender Analysis identified and analyzed the gender risks and impacts of the program and climate change through four main steps:

Scoping: The step includes a scoping process to review relevant literature and data for the project area, interview local experts and data collection with women and other partners, and conduct field visits to understand the project, identify and characterize the project area, and identify stakeholders.


---
**Page 206**
---

including program-affected parties and other interested parties, who may have different concerns and priorities about project and climate change impacts, mitigation mechanisms and benefits.

### Legislative and policy review

The GYA conducted a review of (1) Rwanda's applicable policy framework, national laws and regulations and institutional capabilities relating to gender and youth; (2) variations in country conditions and program context across the affected area(s); (3) relevant gender and youth policies, strategies, plans and programs at the national level; (4) international conventions and treaties; (5) applicable requirements under GCF standards and (6) internationally accepted best practices.

### Stakeholder consultation and analysis

Based on the identification of stakeholders identified in the scoping exercise, the GYA conducted initial consultations with stakeholders to gather information on concerns and priorities about the project and climate change, analyze the outcomes of the consultations and develop a strategy for continuing stakeholder engagement.

### Baseline analysis

Drawing on the scoping exercise, the GYA assembled and analyzed existing information from various sources including the results of the stakeholder consultation and analysis and legislative and policy review, to identify information gaps and ways in which these may be filled. This information was then used to guide the Gender Youth Social Inclusion Action Plan. The details of the stakeholders consulted, including key informant interviews (18), focus group discussions (24), and dietary surveys (30) are available in Annex A. A literature review is available in the Gender Assessment (above) and ESIA (Annex 6).

## 2.0 Gender Issues

There are three key gender-based themes that influenced the design of the Gender Action Plan:

a. **Negative gender and social norms** The most profound barrier for this project is rural norms about the roles of men and women. Whilst the Government of Rwanda has made many advances and has implemented many policies (see Section 3 of the Gender Assessment) to achieve gender equality, there are still significant challenges in terms of changing these deeply rooted gender-biased norms. The consequences of this for this project is far-reaching. Men are generally seen as the head of household with the decision-making powers over all assets and resources within the household (see Section 3 of the Gender Assessment and Jaff et al., 2017). Though female headed households face the same issues and challenges as male headed households, they are disproportionately impacted because of prevalent gender inequality issues (GMO 2016). Women in rural areas have limited access to resources such as land, water and credit. There is a lack of benefits, such as clean farming, casual labor, and plantation projects. Although under Rwanda law, sons and daughters receive equal inheritance rights (Law No: 229/1 of 12/11/1999) the PPF focus group discussions revealed that women are often not aware of this law. Women are also in a position where they depend on marrying a man to gain access to farmland; without a formal marriage, these women have no land tenure. Broadly, these gender and social norms leave most women with limited decision-making powers over resources within the household.

b. **Gender-based violence (GBV)** At the household level where women try to assert independence and achievement is high. For this project, the implications are that trees planted by women become men's property; money gained from selling these plants is very much controlled by men; household products such as food, honey, etc are ultimately controlled by men; and women shouldn't participate in activities without a


---
**Page 207**
---

husband’s permission. Although this seems bleak, this situation is not universal. The 24 CND community focus groups held in the PPF highlighted that many households decide together on how money should be spent: land tenure is broadly seen as joint ownership; and men realize the impact of dwindling fuelwood resources on women and girls. Gender equity is not yet universal and rural culture has a long trajectory to achieving it.

As a result, this program will focus heavily on social and behavior change communications (SBCC) as a mechanism for gender change perceptions towards gender equity. Community members, including community leaders and women and men community influencers specifically will be targeted for sensitization on gender equity in order to shift their attitudes and to build a conducive environment for women’s empowerment. The project will ensure that all activities are designed with the understanding of the development of this project to ensure time constraints, work burden and reproductive responsibilities do not impede their ability to engage in the various activities designed by the project. Women will be required to participate in all aspects of the project including planning, implementation and evaluation. Women in particular will be encouraged to participate in all aspects of the project as they are safe and contextually appropriate. At project start, once communities are selected for implementation, a community assessment will be conducted to identify barriers to women’s participation and solutions to overcome barriers incorporated into programming through an additional screening process outlined in Annex 6. The project ESS Coordinator and Gender Officer will provide support to ensure that all activities are gender sensitive and inclusive of women and girls. The project will also address barriers to ensure their active participation in activities. The project will also get support from NGOs that help men on masculinity and addressing SGVB which will include targeted outreach to members of the community to increase awareness, understanding and acceptance of gender equality and sensitization on the importance of fair access and control of resources, including income. The engagement of community leaders and women and men community influencers to influence more equal use of land and other resources between men and women is also a key focus in men taking over control of earned incomes and targeted for women. Lastly, the project will clearly explain participant selection, intended benefits and how participants can help monitor benefits and risks and reduce risks if they are not satisfied with the project or its outcomes as outlined in the Monitoring and Evaluation. The program will have a safe, accessible Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) for all project stakeholders, particularly women, to access to pursue redress as needed. The project will also collaborate with existing legal and law enforcement agencies to ensure that women’s rights are protected throughout the project. All project staff will be trained and project beneficiaries informed on the purpose and use of the GRM, including reporting gender-based violence. The project will ensure confidentiality of the information and identify appropriate mechanisms for addressing gender-based violence and sexual harassment which will add a layer of protection for individuals who may be subject to gender-based violence. Throughout project implementation, project staff will disseminate information to beneficiaries on how they can use the GRM and seek feedback on how the mechanism is improved.

b. Project access to skills, social leadership and program inclusion. Because of existing gender norms, there is much to do in terms of technical skills of rural women to be able to participate in the project. In addition to that, finding women leaders and building their leadership skills to be at the forefront of rural gender equity is crucial for addressing the root causes of women’s exclusion in land use planning and decision-making. This project however will not just focus on rural women. Ensuring


---
**Page 208**
---

that women play a strong role at all levels of climate programming in the country is important. Thus developing professional networks and internships to provide opportunities to strengthen leadership and technical skills will be incorporated into the program.

### c. Facilitate women's financial autonomy

In order to support rural women to capture financial benefits of this project, this project will incorporate three activities: financial skills building, support in joining cooperatives; and facilitating access to entrepreneurship through financial/entrepreneurship training, access to village savings and loans associations and grants; and mentoring. The project will ensure all training is gender-sensitive and inclusive. Gender equality will be mainstreamed into the training curriculum, content and delivery methods. Flexible training schedules and convenient venues will be used to participate to women's needs. Staff in charge of gender aspects will ensure gender mainstreaming and ensure that projects are gender sensitive.

The project will also use participatory approaches to create an inclusive learning environment and incorporate components on women's empowerment and leadership development, promoting gender equality and active participation of women in the decision-making process. Women who have been economically marginalized independently until shifting norms and household situations reach gender equity for households in adapting to climate change. Within the program, microenterprise, access to finance, beekeeping, and agricultural extension services will be provided to women as well as men. These activities will help build livelihoods within the target rural households and help strengthen resiliency of the rural economy. Further information on women in the value chains targeted by the project, including gender characteristics, composition and roles of women is detailed in the project Feasibility Study where possible and will be refined during project implementation.

#### 1.2.1 Youth Analysis and Key Issues

Rwanda is a young country: 82% of the population is under the age of 40 and 51.5% are 19 or under (NSIR, EICVS 2018; see Table 5). The sex ratio for youth, classified as people from 14-35 years old, is 92 males for every 100 females. The literacy rate for youth is quite high: averaging 91% in urban areas and 76% in rural areas. Youth are more likely linked to wealth, with poorer families having lower capacity (72.4% vs 92%). Larger urban-rural discrepancies are found in computer literacy (28.5% vs 7%) and mobile phone ownership (70% vs 41%).

Employment figures for rural youth indicate that 54.7% are engaged in agriculture, and 32.9% in elementary activities. The rest are in services (7.8%), and very few in managerial, professional etc jobs. According to a recent analysis, youth 'version self-sufficiency achieved through economic independence and the ability to provide for and support their families, and they see this path as most available to them to through self-employment (USDA 2019). The Youth Assessment highlighted key priority areas that youth identified for achieving self-sufficiency:

* Livelihoods and skills development for productive self-employment activities
* Education and skills for entering into the formal work sector
* Reproductive autonomy and health to avoid early pregnancy which is a key hurdle towards economic self-sufficiency

Poverty amongst youth has remained stable since EICVS 4, with about of 30% all of those below poverty level, and 11.3% in extreme poverty. There are substantial gender differences, with young women increasingly vulnerable as they age (see Figures 7 and 8 with data from NSIR’s EICVS 5, 2018). Thus, programming ensuring attention on both young men and young women is vital for rural climate resiliency.

The youth interviewed are very cognizant of these constraints, and many are keen to diversify their livelihoods yet they are most interested in short-term gains. This GCF program intends to seek out vulnerable youth in critical areas of the CND to support entrepreneurship and diversified opportunities to reduce pressure on highly marginalised lands.

### Access to skills building
Many youth attend schools, but training in practical agroforestry, financial management, and forestry is lacking. This program intends to target youth for diversifying their subsistence farming activities into commercial enterprises.

#### Youth leadership and Programmatic Inclusion
Many youths voiced their concerns over not being included in decision-making processes and programming, resulting in key stakeholders not being engaged or consulted. In order to engage the role of women and that of rural farmers and consumers, this entire idea is aligned with the CND to ensure the GCF to understand the needs of the gendered and support long-term tree initiatives. With youth involved in decision- making processes, innovative ideas to involve youth with best practice on government lands and to get youth to appropriate long-term thinking through tree planting as future investments.

## 1.22 Internal program considerations
In addition to programmatic activities with women and youth, this program will also have an internal focus to ensure best practices. These include:

- Avoid perpetuation of gender inequalities and women's exclusion in the agroforestry sector. GEBOD will be designed with a shift towards inclusivity and skills building to facilitate women and youth to join the sectors.
- In addition, women need to be engaged in decision-making bodies of the project itself, including a Steering Committee, which will be at least 50%, and the Project Management Unit (PMU) will have 50% representation of the gendered roles for planning and training increase capacity. The Gender Monitoring Office will be part of a the Steering Committee and along with The National Women's Council and The Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion were consulted on this.
- There is also a need to ensure that women are not left behind in the project, especially at the national and local level. There will be comprehensive consultation and feedback processes with these stakeholders through meetings and workshops to ensure perpetuating gender inequalities is avoided.

### Build partnerships
This GCF project provides a unique opportunity to engage civil society at national and local levels. The team will work with men, women's, and youth organizations to build their capacity in agroforestry and forest management and to support them in the implementation of the project.

#### Gender and Diversity training
Training will be an important component of a large 5-year program. Building online training modules that can be viewed across the CND, and using new platforms like the App Store and Google Play, will ensure that gender diversity is not left behind as training is avoided.

### Staying: Diversity and inclusion are important for the project, and hiring practices at all levels of the program will be reflected in hiring policies. The program management unit will hire a full-time dedicated gender expert and a full-time dedicated youth focal point (both AE staff) and associated costs are included in the project budget. These two staff will participate in all management meetings to support inclusion and diversity, and they will also be part of the GCF Gender, Youth, and Social Inclusion Action Plan. Another key role of these two positions will be to engage civil society


---
**Page 212**
---

partners, particularly women’s, men’s, and youth groups to build capacity and increase the sustainability of achievements during this five-year project. Along with these positions, RFA staff will include a Community Mobilization Specialist and a Community Engagement Specialist who will be in charge of and support project gender mainstreaming. Their responsibilities include reviewing site specific barriers faced by women and men in project activities and identifying ways to address them. In order to support full participation of women, ensuring gender equity in all project activities and where needed help women access the Grievance Redress Mechanisms to pursue redress and connect women with Sangha One Stop Centers in the project area to prevent gender-based violence and provide immediate assistance.

### M&E
Many stakeholder meetings highlighted the lack of community engagement as a key reason for project failures. The project will continue to focus on increasing community engagement and ensure best practice is followed. This includes not only deeper local government engagement but also using a rights-based approach to ensure that communities are at the heart of all interventions. Targets for youth and gender are incorporated into the Gender and Youth Action Plan below and are set as part of the project’s overall targets. All sites will be able and encouraged to actively participate. Exceptions include situations where group composition, such as government officials or community leaders, are outside the project's control or the activity solely targets men, such as massive security operations. In these cases, women will benefit from increased and benefits or assisted natural regeneration activities inside the park far from villages that will take male participants several weeks away from their homes. Overall targets for key activities (i.e., G4.1.15, G4.1.16) have been set as the target will depend on the number of women who participate in project activities takes place; however disaggregated targets per village/site have been set. A project baseline will be conducted and baselines for all targets will be determined at project onset.

## A21. Executive summary

Rwanda's Congo-Nile Divide (CND), an area of 444,800 hectares, is a high-elevation landscape of remnant natural forest reserves embedded in a mosaic of intensively managed agricultural land. This ecologically critical piece of the Albertine Rift, one of Africa’s most biodiverse regions, rises from 900m to 4,507m. The CND separates the drainage basins of the Congo and Nile Rivers. It is part of the Albertine Rift, which is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, containing more than half of Africa's birds and 40% of its mammals. At its highest elevations, the region is crowned by the Volcanoes, Gishwati-Mukura, and Nyungwe National Parks, containing Rwanda’s only mountain gorillas and chimpanzees. The CND also contains a high diversity of plant species, with high levels of endemism (species found nowhere else on Earth) and dozens of threatened species, including populations of mountain gorillas and chimpanzees. Nyungwe has been recognized as one of the six highest priority protected areas in Africa by the World Wildlife Fund (Plumptre et al., 2016). Though covering barely 5% of the country, this archipelago of protected forests is of critical importance.

* It is globally recognized high biodiversity values [2,3].
* Its role in Rwanda’s acclaimed ecosystem offerings serving as the primary source of Rwanda's foreign revenue and as a major economic development driver.
* The CND provides water for 10 million people living on the eastern side of the continent containing more than half of Africa's birds and 40% of its mammals. At its highest elevations, the region is crowned by the Volcanoes, Gishwati-Mukura, and Nyungwe National Parks, containing Rwanda’s only mountain gorillas and chimpanzees.
* The CND also contains a high diversity of plant species, with high levels of endemism (species found nowhere else on Earth) and dozens of threatened species, including populations of mountain gorillas and chimpanzees. Nyungwe has been recognized as one of the six highest priority protected areas in Africa by the World Wildlife Fund (Plumptre et al., 2016). These values and services are already compromised by a combination of anthropogenic and climatic factors; they will be much more severely threatened by the potential negative feedback loops associated with projected climate change impacts. The Project will promote an ecosystem-based approach to forest protection and restoration that will enhance the resilience and function of forests in the CND, including functionally linking isolated forest fragments. Through these approaches, the Project will protect, restore and rehabilitate forest ecosystems, enhancing biodiversity and reducing high fire intensity.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V6.0 | PAGE A

## increasing the provision of critical ecosystem services to strengthen adaptation of vulnerable communities

The CND landscape supports nearly one-third of Rwanda's population on barely-one-fifth of its land base. Average population density is 736 people/km², with some districts now exceeding 1,000 people/km²[1]. The high population density and steep slopes have led to widespread deforestation and the degradation of subsistence farmers' while high rainfall has historically permitted generally sufficient food production, the region's rugged topography requires farming on extremely steep slopes. With more frequent extreme rainfall events in recent years, soil erosion has become a major problem, leading to sedimentation in rivers, lakes, and floodplains[2]. Between 2013-2016 heavy rains generated landslides that killed at least 174 people and displaced over 58,000 others. The CND is also vulnerable to droughts, which are becoming more frequent as raised bed cultivation systems in the CND's many valleys and surrounding bottomlands and many hectares of crops being washed away annually[3]. An estimated 1.5 million tons of fertile soil are lost annually to erosion.

CND forests are essential to the region's climate resilience. Since independence, the total natural forest cover has declined 40%, from 219,000 ha to 130,700 ha[4], mostly from episodic planned excisions as well as uncontrolled deforestation and degradation of remaining forests. The CND is one of Rwanda's most important forested areas. Of the original 32,586 ha in the 1980s, now only 3,460 ha remains as natural forest; almost a 90% loss (see Annex 2). In comparison, the Volcanoes and Nyungwe boundaries have been stable for decades. The recent cover decline is largely due to human activities such as agriculture, charcoal production, and firewood collection in forest, particularly for its land stabilization and other ecosystem services within the CND's most vulnerable lands and dependent communities.

IPCC models predict rising temperatures and increasingly intense precipitation events for the CND through 2050. The most significant potential implications are especially threatening for smallholders farming on steeply heavily deforested slopes, where they are most exposed to landslides, leading to loss of crops, homes, and livestock[5]. In addition, the high population density severely limits their options for relocation in the event of disaster. This is particularly true for women who, until very recently, had fewer legal land rights than men. The expected 2°C increase in temperature by mid-century will likely lead to a significant reduction in the suitability of the CND's current crop selection and management practices for future farmers. An increase of this scale would also dramatically alter the optimal ranges for tea and coffee production, introducing potential competition between these two crops.

This project is designed to sustain and expand critical forest ecosystem functions in the CND, and ultimately enhance the resilience of the vulnerable communities who depend on them. This will be done by strengthening the capacity of local communities to manage their forests more effectively while also promoting and integrating climate adaptation strategies, based on the latest science, through coordinated planning at the national and district levels. It will also protect, restore, and expand natural forest in and around


---
**Page 227**
---

The core national parks; consolidate and expand some smaller but critical "stepping stones"18 of remaining natural habitat between these national parks (mainly small forest patches and wetlands/ riparian areas); improve the landscape linkage function of key high altitude landscape linkages between the protected areas, with a focus on improving connectivity for wildlife movement. This will also provide opportunities for reforestation forests on steep slopes; silvopastoral interventions on cultivated pasture; and agroforestry interventions in regenerative agricultural areas. Complementary activities will address key drivers of deforestation and forest degradation, including the promotion of sustainable land management practices, income-generating climate-resilient crops, as well as strengthening supportive financial services.

Project interventions will include 10,000 ha of land (including both forest and silvopastoral sites) under project implementation. The project will directly benefit approximately 24,212 people in CND communities on farm plantations, directly benefiting 1,254,242 people (654,404 women) in CND with more climate resilient livelihoods from reduced exposure to landslides, floods and soil erosion and more knowledge on climate resilience. The project will also indirectly benefit approximately 937,800 people through improved agroforestry quality materials and improved ecosystem services. The project will also indirectly benefit 9,260,745 people nationally primarily from the education and outreach program on climate change and gender equality. The total mitigation impact from avoided deforestation and reforestation/ restoration and adoption of improved cookstoves is estimated to be 1,084,291 CO₂ eq by 2040.

* **Climate baseline and current impacts**

The climate of western Rwanda and its CND landscape features conditions highly supportive of tropical montane forests, rich biodiversity and human activities alike. Despite being located deep in the tropics just south of the equator, the relatively temperate CND landscape, mostly above 2,000 meters, ensures relatively cool temperatures through the year (Figure 1).

![](https://example.com/image.png)

| Figure 1(left): Topographic map of Rwanda with riverine drainage channels overlaid. Source: Rwanda (2019). | (right) Congo Nile (Modified by the 350 m elevation contour line showing the present and projected future extent of CNDs in Rwanda. |

Rainfall is abundant for nine out of 12 months, while the mid-year dry season adds dynamic character to phenological cycles of flora and fauna activities and agricultural practices (Figure 2). Prior to landscape conversion for agricultural purposes, continuous dense forest cover yielded augmentation of precipitation through fog interception and increased evapotranspiration, which in turn supported a rich diversity of plant assemblages. The forests also maintained slope stability in steep terrain and yielded percolation and groundwater recharge rather than direct runoff of heavy precipitation. Such conditions are now constrained to the CNDs, where only 10% of Rwanda's total land area is forested (Figure 3). Only about 5% of the CNDs account for just 97% of Rwanda's total land surface. These are Rwanda’s only remaining montane forests yet represent

The regional warming of the climate over the past half-century coincided with widespread forest conversion to agriculture and other land uses in central Rwanda. The resulting landscapes are more open, less complex, and often mimic the landscape mosaic, whereby only the protected forests will retain much of the past climatic character while converted landscapes are likely to be significantly warmer by day, have reduced cloud cover and a higher frequency of extreme weather events. These changes are expected to increase the number of days carrying capacity of warmer air (7% increase per °C warming). Ongoing climatic warming promotes increasingly intense short period rainfall, which acts synergistically with landscape conversion on steep slopes to promote landslides. The CND is characterized by high topographic relief and a complex terrain generally (Figure 4). With its high topographic relief, the CND is highly susceptible to soil erosion. This has been exacerbated in recent years as the region has experienced some of the highest rainfall levels ever recorded over western Rwanda. Between January and June in 2018, landslides caused more than 200 mortalities, and in May 2020, 65 deaths from landslides and flash flooding occurred during a single night of storms focused on the eastern slopes of the CND.

Figure 4: Intensity of soil erosion in Rwanda assessed for the year 2015. Source: NISR: National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda, 2016. The figure shows that the highest intensity of soil erosion occurs along both the east and west sides of the CND landscape. Source: Ngamirizimana et al., 2018.

Wildfire occurrence in forested lands exacerbated by climatic warming increasingly mounts concern globally; and, while fire is a natural process, it has been linked to loss from burning. Absence of fire-adapted flora in CND highland forests, however, suggests that fire has not been a major selective force within the landscape for millennia. The Nguruwe Forest National Park (NFNP) was established as a conservation area with ecological imprint that remains evident 25 years later, as burned areas revegetated with dense ferns rather than replacement forests.37 representing a net loss of about 12% of Nyungwe’s forest cover and corresponding loss in biodiversity. The Nguruwe Forest National Park (NFNP) was established as a conservation area with ecological imprint that remains evident 25 years later, as burned areas revegetated with dense ferns rather than replacement forests.37 representing a net loss of about 12% of Nyungwe’s forest cover and corresponding loss in biodiversity.

Cloud base altitude, which is highly influential in CND montane forest ecology and species composition, is likely to be reduced by climate change. This will increase the risk of fire and facilitate conversion of forests to agricultural lands. Fire interception by vegetation augments mountain precipitation in central African tropical montane cloud forests (15%), so highland forest loss by human action therefore represents a local reduction to the ecosystem services (watermaster provision).

Projected climate change impacts

Temperature increases: Localized projections for the CND landscape of climatic changes for coming decades, generated for the most recent IPCC assessment, present a strong consensus on temperature increase for the next two decades. The magnitude of net temperature change by late-century, and the tendency towards more extreme weather events, is less certain. Projected precipitation trends are also unknowable at present, but a large number of climate model simulations show common patterns, whereby divergence in possible temperature outcomes will only become apparent around 2040 (Figure 5). These projections are based on the RCP8.5 scenario.

There is also major inconsistency between CMIP model suites. As assessment for western Rwanda from CMIPs under RCP 8.5 comparing historical and mid-century outputs suggested rainfall decreases of 5–10% in the period 2036 to 2065, while the CMIP5 ensemble suggests increases of up to 40%. The output from these two CMIP ensemble compilations for western Rwanda differ, but the reversal from drier to wetter gives low confidence in the utilization of precipitation predictions specific to the CND H derived from global models.

To generate more refined results, Grimit et al. (2020) performed regional simulations of East African climate at ultra-fine, convective-following scale (WRF model at 3.3 km model resolution); these were based on the global CESM1-LE simulation and used a nested domain approach. The WRF model was configured to optimize party with regional climatic station data. The resulting high spatial resolution output suggests a strongly amplified rainfall signal over the 21st century over western Rwanda relative to the CMIP5 ensemble mean for RCP 8.5 (Figure 9). **Precipitation intensity changes:** Due to well-understood physical properties of the atmosphere, as warming progresses short-period rainfall rates and individual storm totals, especially for the fraction of higher-end events that can cause flash flooding and promote landslides, will increase and should amplify very rapidly. The results from EAGLE simulations show that increases in mean annual precipitation and heavy precipitation suggest an upward trend is now underway (Figure 8). Forthcoming increases are most pronounced for November through January. Such increases in heavy precipitation events are to be expected under a warming climate, and will likely increase the frequency of flooding, landslides, and other extreme occurrences and major contributors to soil erosion intensity.

Drought-dry spells. Warming will also increase the propensity for vegetation to desiccate during dry spells, intensifying droughts and increasing their duration. The capacity of air to extract moisture from landscapes through direct evaporation and evapotranspiration of vegetation will also increase exponentially as temperatures rise. This means that land surfaces and vegetation will dry out more quickly between rainfall episodes, leading to increased frequency and severity of droughts. As the water cycle intensifies, both natural and human systems depend upon, total rainfall must increase in proportion to intensifying evaporation rates. The CMIP5 multi-model ensemble projections indicate that a considerable balance may indeed be maintained through at least mid-century (Figure B). Under the full range of emissions scenarios considered, there is almost no change in ensemble means through mid-century.

A model satellite scale for assessing drought potential at daily-seasonal times scales is the Vapour Pressure Deficit (VPD). This is an absolute measure of the difference between the water vapor content of the air and its saturation value, and as such, represents a direct metric of the ability of the atmosphere to extract moisture from the land surface. High resolution VPD predictions for present day, mid-century and late-century are shown in Figure 10. Annual cycles of VPD for model grid points high in the Nyungwe Forest and at lower elevation Kigali east of the CND both show remarkably little variation in VPD over the course of a year (Figure 10). Due to the low rainfall regime, the annual cycle is not as pronounced as in other parts of Rwanda. The VPD values are consistently low in Nyungwe throughout the year for the three decade time periods considered here. In contrast, the mid- and late-century projections show that the VPD values during the dry season are four times higher than in Nyungwe during the mid-year dry season (20 vs. 5 hectopascal pressure deficit). This represents a favorable outcome over several decades to come for the CND in terms of limiting desiccating conditions on the slopes of Mount Bugesera and the surrounding areas.

Precipitation seasonality. The annual cycle of climate along the CND sees abundant rainfall for much of the year interspersed by a marked dry season in the June-August months when rainfall becomes light and sporadic. This is reflected in the VPD values, which are lowest during this period due to high relative humidity and resultant runoff. While highland topography largely explains the enhanced rainfall along the CND, the


---
**Page 238**

**(D) PROJECT-PROGRAMME INFORMATION**

occurrence of the dry seasons occurs region wide irrespective of terrain elevation (Figure 11). This finds explanation in the seasonal north-south migration of an equatorial band of enhanced cloudiness and rainfall known as the Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). The slight reduction in rainfall experienced over the CND during the mid-20th century is consistent with a general drying trend observed across Africa, but the north in Uganda; conversely, the more defined mid-year dry season along the CND spanning June through August is associated with enhanced southwesterly airflow that effectively pushes the zone of atmospheric convection further north.

In this light, an unusual finding from the EAGLE project's high-resolution modeling studies is that the CND landscape has a heightened risk of major change in climate seasonally. By the 2055-64 period the mid-year dry season will be replaced by a wetter season, and the mid-year wet season will become drier. The higher emissions scenario may make this seem implausible; it is highly dissimilar from mid-century predictions of the consensus of global models, which sustain the dry season. It finds corroboration, however, in a new study that suggests the CND landscape could be more sensitive to climate change than previously thought and be a source of uncertainty for projections of changes in seasonal timing, and that potentially impactful changes in seasonal rainfall may occur "quite suddenly." Such an eventuality is exceptionally difficult to plan for, and since it would only come to fruition well after the project period. If at all, additional studies could be conducted to provide needed guidance.

Climate risks, vulnerability and impacts

Without strategic actions to confront mounting stresses borne by climate change interacting with unsustainable land-use practices, the CND would doubtless undergo a profound transformation over coming decades with significant loss of biodiversity and ecosystem services, reducing agricultural potential, severe hydrological changes, and increased risk of natural disasters. The most immediate threat is likely to be the accelerated desiccation of the lower forests protecting forested headlands-off, arrivals of pests, pathogens and invasive species, and conversion to grassland. Current cultivation practices in coffee plantations are already under stress as crops like Arabica coffee will be subjected to increasing pressure to convert protected forests to farmland. Where climatic changes will act as increasingly mounting stresses, unsustainable land use and climate change will interact to cause a rapid decline of the forested headlands that protect against landslides. This characteristic much of western Rwanda will experience intensifying erosion and risk of landslides, while built infrastructure such as road and bridges will be overwhelmed since they were engineered to withstand rainfall intensity and frequency in the past. The increased frequency and intensity of heavy rainfalls will increase flash flooding frequency, as time progresses and temperatures steadily increase. Precipitation intensity will increase for short periods of time, which will cause flash flooding and promote landslides. This is certain to occur, is probably already discernible, and likely to amplify very significantly over time as warming progresses. This ties directly to landslides in particular, where the steep slopes and significant base erosion to date and the CND's elevated vulnerability due to high topographic relief and deforested slopes makes this hazard of paramount concern to address (Figure 12).

![](https://example.com/image.png)

Figure 12. Rwanda landslide susceptibility map showing past observed landslides. Source: Ntengyoma et al., 2018.[12]

Significant temperature increases are almost certain to continue for decades to come, and will have mounting impacts on both natural and human systems along the CND, and some are already discernible. Over every kilometer of elevation increase in Rwanda, temperatures decrease by approximately 5.5 °C per kilometer of elevation increase[13], so a 2 °C of warming expected by mid-century translates to a vertical rise on the order of 473 meters, promoting large uplift displacements of a wide range of organisms.

harvesting and human-induced fires, coupled with climate change impacts, especially landslides, erosion and downstream flooding, have compromised the delivery of critical ecosystem services derived from these forests. A detailed spatial analysis of biodiversity in the Congo-Nile Divide was conducted to delineate priority and other areas for conservation. The analysis is based on a systematic conservation plan using MARKAN decision support software.

The key analyses involved identifying and mapping the remaining natural areas of forest and other ecosystems, including those that are threatened by climate change impacts such as landslides in Rwanda's connectivity and bottlenecks analyses, and evaluating ecosystem threat and protection levels. The analysis thus built in landscape connectivity, climate change refugia, biodiversity values, ecosystem services and so on.

The final outcome of the MARKAN and Condatis connectivity analyses split the CND domain into four major landscape categories with a set of priority implementation areas, each with their own place-bound project implementation strategy. These include: (i) to protect forested slopes and riparian areas; (ii) to implement biodiversity-friendly agroforestry to reduce landslides, erosion and downstream flooding. Over and above these place-bound interventions are the overarching goals of promoting the sustainability of rural livelihoods and protecting montane forest in Rwanda's CND landscape.

The Systematic Conservation Plan analyses covered a range of biodiversity features, including:

- Terrestrial ecosystems, including their IUCN Red List threat status and protection level. The analysis focused on identifying priority remaining intact areas, based on the development of a map of ecological connectivity.
- Protected Areas, Protected Forests and Protected Wetlands. All the identified ecosystems to be protected for generation are included.
- Climate change scenarios used as projected changes in bioclimatic envelopes under a range of climate change scenarios.
- Identified biodiversity features such as areas and bottlenecks.
- Hydrological process areas - Rivers and Streams, including buffers.
- Hydrological process areas - Wetlands and Lakes, including buffers.
- Hydrological process areas - Groundwater.
- Landscape process areas - Steep slopes (over 55%) which are most important for minimizing erosion and landslides risk.

Individual species were not separately considered in the assessment as all key species are tightly linked to their underlying intact habitat (in particular intact forest patches, as well as wetlands and riparian areas); and as such, the SCP methodology is designed to be applied at a landscape scale. The SCP methodology involves conservation areas; the SCP methodology always attempts to be spatially efficient by meeting conservation targets in as small an area as possible, while avoiding conflict with other land uses, at the lowest possible cost to society.

Results of the MARKAN spatial analysis:

The MARKAN landscape prioritization (Figure 13), which builds in landscape connectivity, climate change refuge, biodiversity values, ecosystem services, and social costs (in terms of avoiding, where possible, areas with high forest population density, agriculture etc.), splits the landscape into four key planning categories (Figure 14):

- Core Protection Areas (CPA): Nodes that are critical for maintaining landscape connectivity. These include well-managed forests which include Voskopoe, Githuri-Makutu and Nyungwe National Parks. Priority activities include strengthening PA management and sustainability, rehabilitation and restoration of natural forests, other conservation-oriented land use activities that reduce stress on PAs and increase their resilience to climate change (e.g., agroforestry), energy efficient stoves (which are sensible for some patches of forest restoration and beekeeping) and supporting sustainable biodiversity compatible activities (e.g. improved beekeeping). These nodes also include buffer areas around the National Parks.

- Steppe landscapes: These are key landscape linkages and hotspots in the farming landscape that require afforestation on steep slopes and riparian areas to link the CND at a landscape scale. Complementary land use activities such as agroforestry, beekeeping and energy efficient stoves can be sensible for some patches of forest restoration and protection, beekeeping and energy efficient stoves. The Githurai Pastures are a focus for agroforestry on pastoral land to increase the coverage of trees in these landscapes.

- Landscapes linkages: These are key landscape linkages and hotspots in the farming landscape that require afforestation on steep slopes and riparian areas to link the CND at a landscape scale. Complementary land use activities such as agroforestry, beekeeping and energy efficient stoves can be sensible for some patches of forest restoration and protection, beekeeping and energy efficient stoves. Note that the analysis is based on some level of afforestation in these landscapes but does not imply continuous natural forest corridors or an overall improved species composition and tree coverage (within mixed agroforestry systems). It does not imply a continuous natural forest corridor; as this potential no longer exists, it would be impossible to be possible in this highly used landscape without unacceptable impacts on livelihoods.

- Broader Farming Mosaic: These are broader areas of moderate priority where conservation interventions can be implemented. These landscapes have lower levels of biodiversity and ecosystem services but are likely to be beyond the scope of most project interventions except for those linked to land use planning.

Specific priority areas for a range of interventions were spatially identified, including:

- Agroforestry on private landholdings and communal lands.
- Specific agroforestry priorities on pastoral land (silo-pastoral practices).
- Indigenous shade trees for tea and coffee plantations.
- Beekeeping in National Park buffers and Stepping Stone buffers.

# PROJECT PROGRAMME INFORMATION

## B (2): Theory of change narrative and diagram

The theory of change for this Project is founded on several key principles. Central to all, the CND represents a mosaic of land uses in Rwanda, including forest and farming patches, each dependent on the other. These coupled, biological and socio-economic systems are under great strain due to intense land use, which has led to degradation of both natural and socio-economic systems. The advent of climate change is a forcible driver that intensifies this cycle of degradation, with the resultant loss of key ecosystem services that importantly link forests and people. This project seeks to address these challenges by promoting landscape heterogeneity and ecological connectivity within this mosaic of land uses to promote landscape heterogeneity and ecological connectivity.

The approach to be taken by this Project is therefore based on principles of ecosystem-based adaptation (EBA) and integrated landscape management, which are key strategies for addressing climate change challenges. Climate-aware management of both natural and human-dominated ecosystems – interacting and integrated at a landscape level – can break the cycle of degradation and instead lead to a positive spiral of resilience, conservation, stewardship, sustainable use, and resilient benefits.

In sum, the goal of this Project is that:

* **If Rwanda’s CND landscape of native forests and neighboring farmlands is effectively managed for climate resilience**

Then

* **The CND will comprise an interconnected and interdependent set of globally significant, species-rich natural forests in a matrix of sustainable farms, acting as buffers against damage from extreme weather events; ensuring landscape integrity, stability and adaptability; providing vital ecosystem services and increasing the capacity to sequester carbon; promoting biodiversity conservation; enhancing livelihoods; and the conservation of biodiversity, the national economy, and mitigation of GHGs.**

BECAUSE building the capacity and management of integrated, climate-resilient forests and farming systems will help mitigate the impacts of climate change-induced intensifying cycles of drought, flooding, and landslides that lead to degradation of livelihoods and resultant increased pressure on forest resources.

The status quo and future of the CND’s forests and people are tightly intertwined: both heavily dependent on the natural resources and processes that provide a foundation for their ability to thrive. They represent ecological and socio-economic systems that are importantly coupled in a complex landscape, linked in particular by the ecosystem services they provide (e.g., water regulation, soil conservation, carbon sequestration, biodiversity conservation, and nature-based tourism). At present these services, and the consequent relationships between forests and people – especially those who are most vulnerable in Rwandan society – are deeply

# (D) PROJECT/PROGRAMME INFORMATION

## Strained Forests

Forests have been reduced in extent, fragmented, and degraded by fire[1], overuse of resources[2], and introduction of exotic species[3]. The sharply sloped rural lands of the CND have been farmed more and more extensively and intensively on steeper and steeper slopes[4] and throughout riverine bottomlands. Furthermore, forests are being cleared for charcoal production[5], livestock grazing[6], and to provide fuelwood[7], soil acids[8], flooding[9], provide consistent and healthy water[10], ameliorate microclimate[11], store carbon[12] and biodiversity[13]. The loss of forests has led to increased vulnerability to climate change, reduced resilience of insecurity and constrained the well-being of farmers. Having little access to alternative sources of livelihoods or land use options, farmers are forced into a cycle of deforestation and degradation that is unsustainable for land, fuel, and other forest resources[14]. Such pressures in turn cause further forest loss and degradation and decline in biodiversity – reducing their ability to provide essential ecosystem services to people living in the region. This has led to increased vulnerability to climate change and reduced resilience of insecurity.

Thus, these systems are caught in a negative cycle that has proven difficult to break, despite significant scientific evidence[15] and policy interventions[16]. According to the 2019 Rwanda State of Environment and Outlook Government of Rwanda (GoR) census found that 77% of Rwandan households use wood as their primary fuel for cooking[17].

## Effects of Climate Change

With the effects of climate change, these already strained systems are showing clear signs of breakdown. Increased variability in the timing and intensity of rains along with rising temperatures are causing increased landslides[18] and soil erosion[19], increased desiccation and drought[20], and unpredictable timing for agricultural planting seasons[21]. These effects are further exacerbated by deforestation, which is reducing the amount of carbon stored in remaining forested areas, thereby compromising further the essential ecosystem services that are necessary to provide resilience against climate change. The loss of forests also reduces the capacity of biodiversity in the CND compromise national-level benefits of water provision and quality[22], nature-based tourism[23], the supply of hydroelectricity[24] and carbon storage[25] (see diagram A below).

## B.3. Project (programme) description (max. 2500 words, approximately 5 pages)

Rewandara's CND region is a complex, naturally integrated landscape. Its diverse high-elevation forests capture and store water resources, releasing them in a sustained manner throughout the year to surrounding steep hillside and bottomland farms and plantations, before feeding into the national network of wetlands, rivers, and lakes. The CND flows through the Virunga National Park (VNP) on the border with Uganda in the north, down through Gishwati Mukura National Park (GMNP), to the south end of Lake Kivu and Nyungwee National Park (NNP) on the southern border with Burundi. ### Activity 2: Climate Change Adaptation

This activity aims to ensure that climate change adaptation requirements are fully integrated into planning processes at local, district and national scales. This will involve i) participatory scenario analysis to understand the problems local communities and district officials face in terms of natural disasters (flooding, soil erosion, landslides), ii) a vulnerability assessment for each community, including an assessment of the economic consequences of these problems in terms of ecosystem service demand and development resilience and adaptation capacity; iii) risk management to estimate the impacts on the overall land use and land cover patterns, including forest resources, on flood risks, soil erosion, land degradation and the well-being of local people, especially any disproportionate impacts on women, youth and historically marginalized groups. iv) identification of possible climate change adaptation actions for both adaptation and mitigation; v) prioritization of these actions according to their feasibility and urgency in consultation with local communities, district leaders, and other stakeholders (and vi) preparation of a draft plan for the project. A participatory stakeholder consultation and feedback process will be undertaken to incorporate views of stakeholders at all levels (e.g. civil society; men, women, youth, and historically marginalized people in local communities; district & national government). The final version of the plan will be finalized and approved by the Government of Rwanda.

### 1.3 Local capacity building in land use planning strengthened to integrate biodiversity and climate risks into land use planning and management

Forest data in Rwanda has historically been generated in an ad-hoc fashion™ through the support of external agencies. This precipitates comprehensive consideration of forest and biodiversity data in land-use planning processes. The National Forest Policy, the National Biodiversity Strategy and the National Land-Use Development Master Plan, building governmental capacity in generating and utilizing spatial data to inform decision making is essential. The activities under this output will involve recruitment of experts in forest mapping, climate change modeling, and biodiversity conservation into a national spatial planning unit within government.
