Activity 3.1 | Restore high slope areas (≥55%) as protective forests

In Western Province, a major part of the CND landscape, 80% of the increase in tree planting in recent years has come from private landowners seeking to earn revenue or increase their access to wood based fuel. Based on this trend and the need for sustainable forest management, the project will aim at extending of protective forests and enhancing and restoring forest plantations as key steps to restoring ecosystem function and services, especially under climate change conditions that are expected to cause extreme climatic events and an increasing long-term supply of woody resources (the energy source for cooking) while also contributing to biodiversity habitat, and sequestering 154.721 t CO₂ over 20 years.

The current land use master plan discourages cultivation on slopes greater than 35% and encourages protection of the existing forest cover by planting indigenous tree species. This Project will promote indigenous species in rehabilitating existing forests and establishing new ones on bare lands. This activity will result in highly productive, climate-resilient woodlots and forestland with fully restored ecosystem services. The project will also contribute to the restoration of degraded land through rehabilitation of degraded private smallholder land and district-state land by restoring existing degraded tree stock, afforestation, reforestation, and awareness and capacity building activities.

The Project will support the implementation of the Forest Management Plan (SMPR), as recommended by 2013 forest law. Experiences from pilot PFMUs established under the FMEC project in the districts of Giambi, Galakwe and Rulindo Districts of the Northern Province and Remangamwe District of the Eastern province have demonstrated that PFMs are a viable model for forest management. They provide an opportunity to improve and improvement of living conditions of the PFMU members. Forests are sustainably managed, and all activities are carried out in accordance with the laws and regulations governing forests. The best practice followed because cooperatives supervise all activities with technical guidance from the district technicians. The forests within a PFMU are economically attractive to potential buyers due to good stock at harvestable age. This is because the forest management plan is well designed, and the forest owner knows that he will be able to harvest his timber in time.

It shows that PFMUs established in these areas are also serving as demonstrations to other forest owners supported by other projects in the country. Green AMAYAGA and Green Giambi, and TREPA Projects are some of those examples.

#### Activity 3.2: Develop on-farm agroforestry for high-caloric and indigenous tree species

The extreme land scarcity of the CND precludes smallholder farmers – many of them among the most vulnerable and land-poor of the region – from dedicating any significant proportion of their holdings to tree production, which is a major constraint in terms of food security. Trees that enrich the soil and control erosion when interplanted with ground crops can greatly reduce this conflict.

Under this activity, the Project will facilitate the production of on-farm agroforestry action plans for selected areas where Project activities may lead to reduced access to resources. The action plans will follow the methodology introduced by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and IUCN and already tested in the country by the former Ministry of Natural Resources, as recently modified and applied for the Gatsibo Forest Landscape Restoration Project. These action plans will be based on a participatory forest landscape resource analysis to map degraded land that presents an opportunity for forest and landscape restoration (FLR), which will highlight areas with best potential for restoration; to economic analyses to model the costs and benefits of agroforestry in the selected areas, including the cost of establishing trees and the income generated based on an in-depth assessment of the conditions required to implement the FLR in the selected sectors.

For selected areas where Project activities may lead to reduced access to resources, the Project will undertake a participatory forest landscape resource analysis (FLRA) to map degraded land that presents an opportunity for implementation and design an Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) to guide implementation. This ESMP will include an access restriction mitigation plan, if deemed necessary. The methodology used in this FLRA is based on the WRI/IUCN methodology as modified and applied for the Gatsibo approach appropriate. These documents will be based on materials contained in Annexes.

Drawing on experience with high-elevation species identified both in Rwanda and across East Africa, the Project will support the following sub-activities:

#### 3.2.1 Identify sub-areas of intervention for agroforestry dissemination in the CND

#### 3.2.2 Introduce and raise awareness of agroforestry in target communities

#### 3.2.3 Develop the capacity of extension agents at district/sector level and NGOs to support adoption of agroforestry technologies

To respond to the growing pressure on natural resources and increase the local community's resilience to climate change, this Project will:

- Key drivers of deforestation by creating alternative livelihood pathways for youth and women through ecotourism and income-generating, climate-resilient crops, as well as strengthening supportive financial services.

This project will employ a market systems development approach that encompasses business coaching, value chain development, and access to finance. ### Activity 3.2.1: Develop agroforestry related value chain for markets access.

Macadamia production in Burundi is linked to fuel production in terms of firewood, charcoal, and timber for construction. However, to further strengthen community resilience to climate change, there is a need to introduce fruit and nut trees that have high economic value in the agroforestry system to generate more income opportunities for households.

Though women-headed households face the same issues and challenges as male-headed households, they are less likely to be included in income-generating activities and are disproportionately impacted by climate change. Macadamia is a particularly suitable crop for women because it can be grown on small plots that have been identified as high economic value crops with high market potential, and the economic benefits of developing macadamia as a particular cash crop will be shared equally between men and women.

In addition to the short-term benefits from macadamia production, the long-term benefits include: (i) the short term, short term crops like chili and French beans will be promoted to encourage smallholder farmers with limited land resources (less than 0.5 ha) to create additional, more quickly generated income and incentive towards adoption of better farming practices; Regular income will help vulnerable communities to cope with climate variability and shocks.

The identified agroforestry value chains have market potential and potential for intercropping with short-term horticultural vegetables and fruits while providing further impacts on carbon sequestration, nutrient value, and soil fertility. Macadamia is a high-value crop that can be grown in the agroforestry system to mitigate climate impact while generating long-term economic benefits to the most vulnerable community members within the CND region.

For each identified activity, specific, identified bottlenecks will be addressed while focusing on specific product-place combinations within the CND. Especially, attention will be on enhancing the quality and quantity of production in sync with particular demands from market niches, development of various models to support smallholder farmers in accessing markets, and promoting value addition activities that can generate off-farm jobs to absorb a good number of landless and other vulnerable groups of youth and women.

* Macadamia: A low volume, high-value export crop; In-country processing creates jobs for women and youth. Two hundred and four trees cover one hectare, and one mature tree produces up to 60 kg of macadamia nuts per year with an income of 25,000 FRW per kilogram. Furthermore, every tree must be supported by a minimum of two fruiting trees. Macadamia is a long-term crop that requires three years to be planted and harvested while waiting for macadamia's fruit maturity (9). The global demand for macadamia outweighs the available supply, which presents a huge business opportunity for macadamia producers in Burundi. The global market for macadamia nuts is expected to reach 10% of global demand and the global market for macadamia is expected to further expand from $1.7 billion to $2.36 billion by 2027. **Activity 3.2.2.3:** Facilitate access to output markets for vulnerable farmers

Lack of access to the market is a challenge to smallholders; only about 10% of agricultural households have access to organized markets. The main barriers to market access for smallholder farmers are mainly attributed to lack of access to market information, failure to meet market requirements, or undeveloped value chains. Some of the challenges also stem from poor quality and poor produce aggregation, which limits their ability to compete in the market. To address these issues, the project will focus on improving quality and capacity, and in creating market linkages with off-takers or buyers through market information. The project will work closely with producer organizations and other stakeholders required to practice modern farming, with the main objective of establishing long-term business relationships with markets/buyers. A focus on financial literacy and community initiatives will also mobilize domestic investment for smallholder farmers to access credit facilities, help them to create innovative financial products, and support improved data collection and measurement of outcomes.

Furthermore, through producer organizations, the project will develop an inclusive business model to improve produce aggregation and supply coordination and to increase farmers' bargaining power and ultimately market access. The project will also work with off-takers to ensure that they have sufficient capacity to absorb the increased volumes of agricultural products from smallholder farmers.

To further strengthen market access, the project will develop innovative market access approaches such as "it takes two to trade," which focuses on understanding the challenges and weaknesses that limit demand (thus creating a win-win situation). The project will also work with producer organizations to identify their weaknesses to build sustainable market access. The project will also build on the national digital agriculture strategy, which is currently being implemented in the Kajiado district through an IFAD-funded project: Strengthening Agriculture Resilience through Mobile Technology (SMART). This approach is particularly customized to poor, rural, and hard-to-reach farmers who do not own smartphones.

To implement this, the project will identify and select two buyers/off-takers for each selected value chain based on market needs and link them to farmers and farmer organizations. The eligibility criteria for businesses that can be considered as off-takers are: (i) have a minimum of 10 years' experience in business; (ii) have a minimum of 50 employees; (iii) have a minimum turnover of KES 2 million per annum; and (iv) have a minimum capital base of KES 3 million. The project will organize periodic market linkage events and business-to-business (B2B) workshops through established value chain platforms. Additionally, the project will create a clear link between market access and financial inclusion by providing smallholder farmers with access to credit facilities and other forms of working capital for aggregation and marketing. Various models will be developed including tripartite agreements (buyers, producer organizations, or financial institutions) to increase confidence among partners and stakeholders.

The activity will work to scale up the market system developed using the Output 3.2 inception report on beneficiary persons and stakeholder engagements to facilitate market system growth within the selected value chains. The project will provide training, business development services, and advisory services to scale up the market system developed using the Output 3.2 inception report on beneficiary and stakeholder

## B

### Group Savings and Credit Unions

Group members follow clear rules and regulations which are known and adhered to by all group members.

Groups consist of a limited number (10-25) of people who have freely chosen to work together, and offer self-managed savings, insurance, and credit services in remote rural areas. Poorer segments of the community often participate in these groups because they do not have access to formal financial institutions or can save to purchase agricultural inputs, such as seeds, fertilizer or equipment. Savings groups may also provide mutual assistance for group members, such as medical insurance or loans to members in need.

Savings groups have transformed marginalized communities by mobilizing local savings, which provides members with a means of saving and accessing credit. These groups are characterized by their informal nature, crucially, re-build social networks, solidarity and trust. Savings group participants often do not have regular savings accounts at formal financial institutions or access to other segments of the community. Women are regularly involved in savings groups and have high participation rates. Saving group participants often come from the same socioeconomic background and know each other.

### Activities of saving groups include:

- **FINANCIAL:** The group establishes a reserve, fixed for a period that each group member will bring to the savings account. The allocation and management of these savings can vary according to the needs of the members or is used to support group activities.
- **EducaTion:** The group provides education on financial matters. Loans are modest and repayable in the short term. Interest rate is fixed by members. At the request of the group, these credits are renewable almost automatically if there is no problem and if the amounts are within a ceiling set by the group.
- **Social:** The group not only improves the lives of its members financially but also socially as members learn to trust each other and build relationships that can be used for mutual support in times of concern. The group further builds a small social fund to help group members in distress. Each group agrees on the amount to be saved, usually a smaller amount than the amount for regular savings. This is often used by groups to provide financial assistance to members who have experienced group member expenses for things such as funeral costs or medical treatment and are only used if agreed upon by all group members.

In case of emergency, group members can access services providers, which most members cannot afford. Group members agree to mutually guarantee each other (co-guarantees) when taking a loan. If a member does not pay, the group ensures repayment for him/her. The group uses moral pressure to force repayment and therefore there is no need for formal financial institutions or collateral as security. These loans are often seen as financial transactions. The internal character assessment for group members is important.

The project will strengthen the capacity of saving groups and link them to more formalized financial institutions. The project will further enhance financial education and direct protection principles.

This model is more convenient and more accepted by most women who cannot afford collateral loans, such as mobile phones or cellphones. These are often used for savings and can be accessed at any time. Specific attention will also be paid to women's participation in other project financial products that will be developed as well as asset-based activities.

The project seeks to help saving groups to reduce time and cost spent to access their savings, thereby facilitating transactions with formal financial institutions. Solutions such as "push and pull technology" (i.e., payments using cell phones, commonly referred to as "mobile money") have proven to be useful and convenient for savings groups to send and receive money.

#### Activity 3.3.2 Set up and manage savings groups, enhance asset building

To strengthen access of local smallholder farmers in financial literacy and access to finance, farmers' cooperatives will be assisted and supported in setting up saving groups. Savings groups are a proven and effective approach to the financial inclusion of the most vulnerable and are increasingly recognized as one of the best ways to provide financial services for the poor. The project will work with existing groups and build on its savings approach. Saving groups create a platform for linkage with financial institutions and other business development services. Further, savings groups are recognized for enabling high levels of female inclusion in group activities and decision-making processes. Group members' relationships are strong; it forms low lending risks for MFIs since members mutually reinforce each other's repayments.

Once grouped, small saving group members, especially women, grow from accessing microfinance loans to become more financially literate and empowered. Members are responsible and trustworthy; increasingly, members are able to start accessing individual loans, gradually building to larger loans and are able to open individual savings accounts at financial institutions.

Members of a saving group will be self-selected and the saving group will be managed by its members.
- Knowledge of one another and similar economic background
- Clear rules for how money in the group will be held
- Reputation for honesty and reliability
- Ability to attend all meetings on time and follow rules
- Have a mobile phone or access to internet
- Be able to buy at least one share each week (or time set by the group)
- Be able to repay loans on time

Most saving groups are informal, unregistered, democratic, and structured groups that have constitutions and clear rules. Members do not enter into contractual arrangements for their membership. Record-keeping is based on simple passbooks in which each member's savings and loans are recorded; all transactions are documented.

Farmer savings groups (FSGs) will be created within cooperatives and farmers will decide which group to join. Groups will set up governing rules and constitutions (savings, meetings, etc.), and criteria for new members. Special attention and particular attention will be given to social inclusion (including vulnerable communities and landless people).

### B.S Justification for GCF funding request

Rwanda has achieved remarkable social, political, and economic progress over the past two decades. The country’s economy has grown above average compared to its peers and the rest of the world, achieving growth rates of more than 8% annually, with a 9.4% growth rate in 2019[17]. However, the economy is which


---
**Page 513**
---

**GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V 6.0 | PAGE 72**

B

dependent on nature-based tourism and agriculture is extremely vulnerable to external shocks, including climate change.

Climate change is likely to increase variability in crop yields and agricultural production, cause severe flood damage to physical infrastructure, reduce labor productivity, and impact demand for tourism(1). The recent COP26 report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) projects that global average sea levels can drop by 5–7% below baseline in multiple years by 2050(2), with negative impacts on private consumption, exports, and government revenues. By strengthening resilience to climate change, Rwanda can achieve its development goals and reduce the vulnerability of its citizens.

The NDCs for Rwanda are articulated in the NDC is estimated to require new investments of US$11 billion, of which close to US$7 billion will be required by 2030.

Rwanda is classified by the UN as a Least Developed Country (LDC)(4) and lacks sufficient public financial resources to implement its climate change and resilient green development objectives. The implications of climate impact for Rwanda demands concerted action and support both locally and internationally to enable the country to achieve its NDCs, which are ambitious in scope and scale beyond what domestic resources required. This Project will allow Rwanda to implement its NDC commitments and pursue its aspirations under its National Development Strategy and Climate Resilience Green Economy plans by promoting trends of high deforestation, allowing for reforestation and sustainable reforestation models that reduce emissions from wood fuel. Rwanda has made an impressive commitment to using forests and forest protection as part of its national strategy to mitigate impacts from climate change, and to provide benefits of biodiversity conservation and livelihood improvements.

Yet, vulnerable citizens' needs, coupled with fragile landscape and forest restoration, will not be met solely with national resources in the rapid timeframe needed to arrest loss of economic assets for households and prevent further degradation of natural resources. Special attention is required on capacity building and training at scale required to increase the resilience of CND communities to the impacts of climate change, and to ensure that they are able to benefit from the project activities. A detailed capacity assessment is currently being developed by the GoRt. The GoRt does not have the financial means to implement all project activities identified to improve climate resilience and requires technical assistance and support. While project implementation will be carried out through existing institutions, it is important that these institutions have the resources required for implementation. The GCF grant investment can help initiate, expedite, and catalyze these critical interventions and assist with alignment of future climate resilience efforts. ## Sectoral monitoring and reporting mechanisms. This will lead to a systematic consideration of climate change risks and adaptation in policy planning that will be sustained beyond the Project. An MoU between key government agencies will operationalize the cross-sectoral planning task force, which will be supported by a national-level steering committee.

### Rwanda has adopted a private-public partnership (PPP) business model to make its national parks operations financially viable. However, as in the rest of the world, national parks and the biodiversity they are intended to protect are threatened by climate change and by the interaction of climate change with other stressors such as human encroachment.

#### Strategies for Long-term Financial Sustainability:
Two specific examples of the Government of Rwanda’s concepts and approaches to financial sustainability that will be key parts of the Exit Strategy are the Tourism Revenue Sharing Program (TRSP) of RDB and the Community Adaptation Fund of FONERWA, the Rwanda Green Fund.
- **Tourism Revenue Sharing Program**: The long-term success of the three protected areas in the CND depends on a substantial extent, on the support of communities living around protected areas. In recognition of this, in 2005 Rwanda established a Tourism Revenue Sharing Program, allocating 5% of gross tourism revenue to each of the three protected areas. This has been extended to other protected areas and national parks through the creation of the Bodogwe Tourism Plan. The FONERWA has given support for the implementation of this program.
- **Community Adaptation Fund**: The Project through RDB will be a Technical Advisor, to work with RDB, MoE, MoH, and the Ministry of Water and Environment (MoWE) on the design and implementation of the Community Adaptation Facility (CAF). The CAF is designed and implemented before the end of the project period to ensure the long-term sustainability of the Project outputs.

The primary challenges identified in the 15-year review are increasing the effectiveness of community engagement, ensuring that the TRSP benefits all communities equally, and improving transparency among community needs. The Gulf is interested in adapting the TRSP Policy to more effectively engage the communities around protected areas. In this regard, the Project will work with RDB and district governments, to increase transparency in the Program, ensure that the most vulnerable community members benefit from the program, and improve the effectiveness of community engagement.

The Community Adaptation Facility (CAF) within FONERWA was developed as part of Rwanda’s NDC Deep Dive: Advancing Financial Innovation to Scale Up Climate Action. The aim of the CAF is to provide grant

funding for community projects that scale up climate resilience. The Project Team will also support the cooperatives and youth-led SMEs in Component 3 to prepare business plans for communities in the CND to join the CAF.

This will mean that The Project will invest in businesses that restore or indirectly halt the degradation and loss of natural resources. These investments are expected to be sustainable and financially viable and are expected to live beyond the lifetime of the project. The value chains, once organized profitably, can continue to grow without further support, while the financial service providers will continue to service savings groups and cooperatives in the CND. The Project will also focus on improving food security by increasing yields through raising the productivity from selected crops, diversifying agriculture towards high-value agroproducts, and strengthening value chains for these products. This will be achieved by providing technical assistance that will attract investments from the private sector in sustainable agriculture and agroforestry. All economic and environmental benefits from the project will be rigorously monitored, captured, compiled and disseminated as lessons learned to promote impact-based business models including investors and NFI with which the project will engage to secure microcredits to beneficiary farmers.

### Budget: $2,000,734

To enhance forest resilience across the CND, through a combination of increased forest cover, improved forest condition, and improved management to reduce degradation and pressure on forests, the project will increase forest cover by 15% in the CND. This will be achieved through reforestation and rehabilitation of large areas previously degraded by fires, securing key remaining natural areas outside PAs and degraded lands within PAs, and improving forest condition across all landscapes. The project will support agencies, districts, and communities to manage forest fires. Community members will be trained in and provided technical assistance and equipment for restoration techniques, establishment, and management of improved forests. This will include the development of a community-based forest management system with staff trained to explicitly consider climate adaptation and gender issues and manage the parks as part of the larger CND landscape. The project will also develop the capacity of key Government ministries and agencies on land use planning for climate resilience.

Additionally, this project will strengthen the livelihoods of landless and/or the most vulnerable households, who are often at risk of losing use of their farmlands, protected areas and resources within protected areas, and those who have been displaced by forest fires. This will be achieved through:

- Helping reduce the risk of crop failure from extreme events like landslides, reduce land and water degradation caused by soil erosion, and increase provision of valuable products like wood fuel.
- To decrease pressure on forests, the project will support the development of alternative livelihoods that can be dramatically scaled up. Community members will be trained in and provided technical assistance for SLUM production and marketing, including the establishment of small-scale enterprises (SMEs) with access to financing from financial institutions (PFIs), and value chain actors/small and mid-size enterprises (SMEs) will benefit from capacity-building to improve their business skills and access to finance, and to strengthen value chains (including through the development of a market for SLUM products). This will include the construction of processing facilities and marketing materials. Vocational training schools and local youth cooperatives will be supported to produce, test, and distribute Tier 2 cookstoves.

### D1. Impact potential

#### Adaptation Impact
- This Project is designed to restore, sustain and expand critical forest ecosystem functions in the CND. More specifically, the project will protect, restore and expand natural forest in and around protected areas (PAs) and other key forest ecosystems such as riparian forests and remaining habitat between these national parks (mainly small forest patches and wetlands/riparian areas); improve the landscape linkage function of high altitude within the protected areas; while at the same time, it will also contribute to improved land use planning and management for agroforestry or plantation forests on steep slopes; silvopastoral interventions on cultivated pastures; and agroforestry restoration in degraded lands. The project will also improve soil fertility through the application of organic manure, and thus increase the water infiltration rate, which increases water recharge which will enhance the resilience of forest ecosystems and smallholder farmers to climate change.
- The establishment of protected areas and other key forest ecosystems will provide a safe haven for species migration to more favorable conditions within this human modified landscape and as a result help build the resilience of biodiversity to climate impacts. Increasing the capacity for species movement across these landscapes will also increase genetic diversity, which is critical in maintaining populations of multiple species that serve as important seed dispersers and insure the long-term viability of forests.
- Project interventions will include 10,000 ha of land (including both forest and silvopastoral sites) under improved, climate-resilient management; and improve agroforestry practices on 3,346 ha of on-farm plantations. The project will also provide training to farmers in the use of organic manure and other results from reduced exposure to landslides, floods and soil erosion and more knowledge on climate risks, value of forests and forest ecosystems, climate adaptation options, access to indigenous and agroforestry quality materials and improved post-harvest services.
- The Project will provide direct benefits to increase the climate resilience of more than 1.5 million of the most vulnerable residents of the CND, including increased adaptive capacity through reduced exposure to flash floods and landslides (which would benefit 90% of the population) and reduced exposure to droughts which beneficiaries 52.2% of female). Indirectly, 2,464,097 beneficiaries in the CND will receive co-benefits from improved and more sustained ecosystem services, including decreased sedimentation leading to improved water quality and quantity; increased soil fertility and reduced erosion; and increased access to renewable hydropower energy at a lower cost, making it preferable to other more detrimental energy sources. The project will also indirectly benefit 320,745 people and create approximately 24,212 job opportunities in the CND.
- The Project will contribute altogether to the restoration of 5,000 ha of intact forest; 2,500 ha of protective forests and 3,346 ha of smallholder farmland. 1,000 ha of pastures and 1,500 ha of riparian linkages. Overall, 275,617 ha of the landscape could potentially be positively impacted by the project as land use planning and management is improved in the CND. The Project will also contribute to improved water quality and quantity; reduced soil erosion would all contribute to improved outcomes beyond the specific sites directly targeted for restoration or improvement. The Project will also contribute to improved biodiversity conservation through the creation of 2,500 ha and hence improved protection of key areas (e.g. steep slopes, riparian areas and protected area buffers) has strong potential to deliver significant mitigation benefits at a landscape rather than a site level. Although the project is located on the priority landscapes covering 13,697 km² it may also benefit due to increased adaptive capacity (achieved through improved land use planning and management of key features such as

## Mitigation Impact – The Project will generate mitigation benefits by delivering sequestration of approximately 224 kt CO₂ eq over the 5-year Project period, which is about ~0.8% of the 28.2M t CO₂ reductions that are projected to be achieved in Rwanda.

- **5,000 ha** of critical intact natural forests will be under improved management for climate resilience, accounting for an estimated total of 596,118 kg CO₂ eq over 20 years.
- **1,000 km²** of degraded land will be restored and managed to increase more sustainable landscape connectivity for forest species, accounting for an estimated total of 4,543 kg CO₂ eq over 20 years.
- **1,500 ha** of riparian lands will be afforested which will contribute significantly to overall landscape connectivity and biodiversity conservation, accounting for an estimated total of 789 kg CO₂ eq over 20 years.
- **2,500 ha** of protective forests and plantations will be established on slopes ~55%, focusing on areas not currently planted in crops, accounting for an estimated total of 193,472 kg CO₂ eq over 20 years.
- Every year, the project will avoid emissions from deforestation and forest degradation over 3.84 ha of smallholder farmland, sequestering 129,096 kg CO₂ eq over 20 years.
- Improved energy efficient stoves will be adopted by 8,500 households, securing 51,071 kg CO₂ eq of avoided emissions.

Overall, there is potential for a significant contribution to GCFI Core Indicator 4.6: hectares of natural resource areas brought under low emission or climate resilient practices. Conversely, an area of 275,617 ha of the landscape could potentially be positively impacted by the project as land use planning, improved natural forest management and restoration activities are implemented on a larger scale than the specific areas targeted to improve outcomes beyond the specific areas directly targeted for restoration or improved management by the project.

### D.2. Payment shift potential

## Potential for scaling-up spatial planning and implementation.

Spatial planning is recognized by the IPCC, the EU and others as playing a key role in climate change adaptation and climate resilient development, but to date, only limited progress has been made on this front in Rwanda. The proposed project will support spatial planning. Adoption of spatial planning across ministries and on national regional and local levels, represents a significant paradigm shift for Rwanda. Pivotal decisions and an ad hoc assembly of sectoral stakeholders have been identified as key barriers to the adoption of spatial planning and development – enabling systemic ecosystem-based multi-sector analysis of land use tradeoffs. The Project will support the Government in overcoming these barriers by providing technical assistance on spatial planning and implementation – one that can be scaled up for use elsewhere in Rwanda and beyond. This will enable better-informed planning decisions, the identification and valuation of nature-based solutions to climate change adaptation, and the development of a national land-use plan (NULUP) for Rwanda. The NULUP is 2030 and nationwide. Communication and collaboration with complementary GCF and other projects in Rwanda will accelerate this process.

### Project Component 1: Knowledge Learning

Component 1 will invest in new technologies and climate smart knowledge to improve national and district planning, scenario analysis and monitoring capacities. In doing so, new mechanisms of coordination and collaboration will be established, and shared across agencies. Component 1 will support the Government in scaling up knowledge learning beyond the existing science of indigenous tree propagation and restoration (particularly in re-establishing rain forest habitat, establishing protective forests on slopes of >35%, and enriching farmlands with indigenous trees). This will include: strengthening the capacity of local communities to use indigenous trees (on-farm and off-farm) not yet in practice. All approaches will include the participation of local farmers, women, and youth; to contribute to knowledge learning beyond the existing science of indigenous tree propagation and restoration. Knowledge generation – and the processes by which it is generated – will be shared across the region. The project is based on collective learning, knowledge generation and dissemination, and the development of national and district level capacity for planning, implementation, demonstrations, monitoring, and evaluation to assess the project activities will inform the implementation of current and future adaptation efforts.

#### Contribution to the creation of an enabling environment

Strengthening the Task Force in Component 1 will ensure that climate change is considered for all sectors’ planning development and investments in the CND and will ensure that planning for climate resilience is addressed. By establishing a mechanism for coordinating and collaborating across agencies, the project will support the Government to implement interventions and will establish partnerships and collaborations that live beyond this Project. Also important, promotion of sustainable financing for each component will help to assure that initiatives will enter into national development plans.

#### Contribution to the regulatory framework and policies

The Project will finance the development of the Integrated Land-use Plan which will be adopted by all ten CND districts as a framework for seeking synergies between rural livelihoods and forest and biodiversity protections, reconciling land use conflicts and ensuring climate resilience. The project will also support the development of an integrated National Land Use Master Plan, ensuring it incorporates climate resiliency, is accurate and relevant to local conditions, and includes a sectoral approach that addresses the needs of all sectors. By addressing sectoral trade-offs and improve climate adaptation planning in the CND, this approach will prove a successful model for application to other regions of Rwanda and to other forest farming landscapes beyond. The proposed Project is aligned with the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including SDGs 5, 13 and 15 and will contribute to the achievement of the SDGs 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10. The Project will promote an ecosystem-based approach to forest protection, restoration, and rehabilitation that includes:

- Reduction of erosion, sedimentation, and landslide risk as a result of restoration of degraded lands;
- Increased number of native trees on farms with improved agroforestry systems, improving biological conservation;
- Increased carbon sequestration potential of plants and soils. While the primary objective of the Project is to achieve 103,852 tCO₂-eq during the 5-year implementation period, and 1,033,276 CO₂-eq over the 20-year Project lifetime;
- Reduced GHG emissions through more fuel efficient cookstove technologies, yielding cumulative savings of approximately 51.971 tCO₂-eq during the 20-year Project lifetime.

The Project will also transform more climate-resilient and productive livelihood models and empower the rural poor, significantly reducing impacts from extreme weather events and increasing their potential for improved wellbeing. Social benefits will include:

- Raised awareness about climate change effects and adaptation in 135,252 people living in the CND;
- Capacity building of ≥52,589 people (at least 50% women), in a wide range of topics aimed at increasing ecosystem and social resilience;
- Creation of an enabling environment for co-designing and co-managing a range of adaptation strategies, indirectly promoting social cohesion among CND villages through joint saving and lending groups;
- Reduced inequality and poverty through increased financial inclusion and improved economic opportunities — especially for women, youth and historically marginalized groups.

### D.4 Needs of recipient

Despite Rwanda’s long economic progress since 2005, poverty remains widespread and pervasive. Overall, 38.2% of the population lives in poverty and 16% in extreme poverty (1). Women are more affected by poverty than men: nearly 47% of female-headed households living in poverty compared with 44.9% of all households. Rural households are more than twice as likely to be in poverty/extreme poverty than urban households. Districts in the Northern and Southern Provinces in the CND region have the highest rates of poverty and extreme poverty in the country.

Most rural households are smallholder subsistence farmers, and because of high population density, high relief terrain and dependence on rain fed agriculture, the residents of the CND are highly vulnerable to climate change. The project will be implemented through a participatory approach that involves extensive stakeholder consultations; communities indicate several socio-economic changes stemming from changing climatic conditions. These include reduced crop yields, increased pest infestations, and droughts, which significantly lead to more widespread malnutrition and extreme poverty, and farmers can barely meet their own families’ needs (2). In particular, women, youth, and historically marginalized people are feeling the impact of climate change most acutely. They have fewer resources with which to adapt and seek new opportunities and are more focused on survival and short-term gains at the expense of education and sustainable livelihood development (see Annexes 6 and 8 for more details).

As a result, the GoR has invested significantly in developing an enabling policy and institutional framework to ensure that climate change adaptation is integrated into all sectors. Rwanda’s approach is a tripartite one: Rwanda is classified by the U.N. as a LDC and lacks sufficient public financial resources to implement its climate change and related adaptation programs. The GoR has therefore developed a multi-stakeholder partnership mechanism to secure Rwanda's priority forests to reduce vulnerability of rural communities to climate risks. The GoR also recognizes that a piecemeal approach to decision making has exacerbated competition over scarce land resources and reduced the adaptive capacity of both ecosystems and rural populations. Additionally, district government staff and community members have limited technical understanding for assessing the complex interactions between forest structure and functions, climate change, and the provision of ecosystem services. Accurate measurement of forest cover and forest type is notoriously difficult in high forest terrain, such as in the CIND[13]. ## D.S. Country ownership

The proposed Project is closely aligned with the NAP[14]'s adaptation priorities: 1) promotion of non-agricultural (albeit forest-based) activities, 2) introduction of species resistant to environmental conditions, and 3) development of firewood alternative sources of energy. It is also aligned with several priority identified in the 2020 NDC: promotion of afforestation/reforestation; improvement of forest management, integrated natural resource management (INRM); and climate change adaptation. The Project will support implementation of the Green Growth and Climate Resilient Strategy and the Rwanda National Strategy for Forests and Land Use Planning (RNSFLUP) 2018-2035. It is also aligned with the government’s strategy to mainstream climate change into sectoral planning, as outlined in the Sector Strategic Plan 2017-2022[15], the Strategy for the Environment and Natural Resources Management (SENRM)[16] and the National Forest Sector Plan 2018-2030. The Project will support government’s intentions to address climate change impacts and mitigation targets by improving forest management. It is also aligned with the national Biomass Energy Strategy (BEST) 2020 which aims to ensure that biomass energy contributes at least 5% of total primary energy supply in Rwanda.

This Project aligns with the forthcoming GCF country program which prioritizes forest management through restoration and protection of natural forests, afforestation and agroforestry, as well as distribution of high-quality timber products[17].

While this Project proposal to GCF focuses on a different geographic area - with specific adaptation needs than land restoration, development of markets and finance mechanism, as well as support to mainstreaming climate change into sectoral planning. The Project will be implemented in the same manner as existing GCF-funded projects: “Strengthening Climate Resilience of Rural Communities in Northern Rwanda[18]” and “Transforming Eastern Province through adaptation” (TREPA)[19] will be applied during the implementation.

## Economic and financial operation (see the Forest Sector Strategic Plan). By restoring smallholder protective forest plantations and organizing them into Private Forest Management Units (PFMUs), this Project will assist with creation of units that are economically attractive to private investors, helping to facilitate future private sector investment in forest protection. The project will also ensure that the land tenure rights and ownership of PFMUs will remain with the state/district governments and smallholders' cooperatives who own forest plantations. RFA in collaboration with RCA and the district government directly implement projects on the ground. The Rwanda Forest Authority (RFA) is responsible for developing, implementing rules and regulation governing each cooperative overseen by the Rwanda Cooperative Agency in case of conflict. The District Government will also intervene in conflict situations.

No excess subsidy will be provided to the private sector; and no private sector investors will be crowded out by these investments. For example, the subsidy/microcredit schemes to facilitate the adoption of efficient cookestoves are undertaken with minimum concessionality. ## Results of the Economic and Financial Analysis (EFA). Following the GCF guidelines for developing the Annex 3 package, the EFA was prepared to assess the economic rationale for the proposed interventions. Consideration is given to three alternative interventions: agroforestry (i), protective forest plantations (ii), fuel-efficient cookstoves (iii), silvo-pastoralism. Best practices in appraisal for public sector projects are followed and the analysis is based on a 20-year horizon with an internal rate of return perspective using a discount rate of 15.44%, which was the lending rate of Rwanda Central Bank. For the three modeled interventions (see table below) the financial NPV is positive and financial IRR is higher than discount rate, indicating that all projects are financially viable. The project will provide an attractive long-term return for farmers or private actors over a 20-year period and will help overcome high up-front investment costs during the project.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUNDING PROPOSAL V4.0 | PAGE 94

The lead beneficiary of this project are individual households... who will participate directly in the project and thus benefit from its implementation. Beneficiaries include all people who can live on land where activities will take place and/or those who will be employed by the project (except EE staff, consultants and implementation and contractual organizations). Dependents of household that directly benefit from the project are also considered as direct beneficiaries and were calculated based on 4.2 average dependents per household.

Adaptation Results Area 1. Core Indicator 2 direct beneficiaries are beneficiaries of activities 2.2.2, 2.2.3, 3.1.1, 11.2

Adaptation Results Area 1. Supplementary Indicator 2.1 direct beneficiaries of activities 3.2.1, 3.2.2, 3.2.4 (excluding 8,500 beneficiaries of cockleworts) and 3.3.2.

Adaptation Results Area 2 Supplementary Indicator 2.2 direct beneficiaries are the total population in landscape implementation sectors of this project.

Indirect beneficiaries broadly refer to all other human populations living within the CNDL districts. More details on calculations are provided in annex 13.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V4.0 PAGE 95

The project will facilitate the development and adoption of an integrated landscape-level planning framework in line with the JAFIT to bring together relevant stakeholders at all levels (national, provincial, districts, private sector and civil society) and across sectors to strengthen inter-sectoral collaboration on the plans. The project will also support capacity development for the national government staff working on FLR and land-use planning (from policy level down to implementation level). The project will also support the Government of Gulf in developing a dedicated SPV within an approach that is aligned with the technical expertise needed to process and integrate sustainable land management into decision-making within and across sectors.

### GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.6.0 | PAGE 96

#### Core indicator: Degree to which CGIAR investments contribute to effective knowledge generation and learning processes, and use of best practices, methodologies and standards.

While GCF recognizes the need for developing an enabling policy and institutional environment for a climate-resilient development pathway, Rwanda has an innovative, scientifically credible system for generating and disseminating information on natural forest cover and condition. There is no system to ensure that this knowledge is incorporated into land use planning or agricultural practices (e.g., agroforestry). The project will design and finance the establishment of a new indigenous forest conservation unit dedicated to collecting data on natural forest cover and condition, and no system exists for integrating spatial planning knowledge into land use plans. The project will establish best practice agricultural and forest management practices in 20,000 ha of land, and create community structures (e.g., farmer groups) that facilitate knowledge and information sharing among community members.

| Rwanda has an innovative, scientifically credible system for generating and disseminating information on natural forest cover and condition. E.7 Monitoring, reporting and evaluation arrangements

The Project’s logical framework outlines the expected results, indicators, means of verification, baseline values and target values at mid-term and end term. The Project Coordinator will be responsible for the overall monitoring of Project progress and reporting to the PSC. A National M&E Specialist hosted under the PMU, supported by EE-based Specialists, will be employed to develop practical guidelines for – and operationalize – a performance monitoring framework. This framework will include: i) establishing a performance monitoring framework to define baseline targets; ii) measuring the indicators at least 1–2 times per year to evaluate the progress of the Project against these baseline targets; iii) reporting on ESMS as well as gender; iv) supporting the PMU in developing a response plan for challenges or issues that may arise during implementation. The National M&E Specialist will support the National M&E Specialist by: i) following guidelines developed by the national M&E specialist to conduct performance monitoring; ii) measuring the program indicators at least 1–2 times per year; iii) ensuring all activities comply with the Project’s ESMP process and procedures; iv) supporting the PMU in developing a response plan for challenges or issues that may arise during implementation. The National M&E Specialist will be supported by a Gender Specialist to oversee and monitor the application of gender disaggregated indicators. The M&E Specialist will conduct at least two visits per year to each project site, with a focus on ESMS and gender. During these visits, the M&E Specialist will cross-check the information provided by EE and beneficiaries in monitoring reports. During each visit, the team will collect qualitative data through interviews with relevant stakeholders, participative workshops and focus groups with beneficiaries. The National M&E Specialist, supported by the EE M&E Specialist will then complete quarterly Project reports outlining progress in each site, allowing for feedback and support from the PMU and ES in case of delay or challenges. M&E, as the AE, will perform supervision missions on year two onwards to monitor the implementation of the project and ensure that the project is aligned with the logical framework. The M&E Specialist will also monitor the destination and use of funds disbursed to the EE – will monitor the Project’s compliance with policies and procedures, as well as alignment with ESMP process and procedures. The PMU will develop a response plan for challenges or issues that may arise during implementation based on the logical framework in the Project, including a report on ESMS as well as gender. The report will be aligned with the modalities set out in the CCF results management framework and its performance measurement frameworks.

As per the AAM, an independent consultant will be contracted to conduct an Interim Evaluation and Final Evaluation. Both will comply with CCP evaluation principles and methodologies including but not limited to: desk analysis, including interviews with relevant stakeholders, data provided by the Project, EE M&E Specialists and Gender Specialist; and participative workshops and focus groups with beneficiaries. The Interim Evaluation will be conducted at year two of implementation and the Final Evaluation at year four. The PMU and PMJ will develop a management response to the recommendations along with an implementation plan, and the PMJ will monitor implementation of the recommendations. The Final Evaluation will be an independent assessment of Project performance against its contributions to a paradigm shift and enabling environment.

# RISK ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT

## F.1 Risk factors and mitigations measures

### Selected Risk Factor 1 - Lack of coordination, institutional resistance, and regulatory barriers to mainstreaming climate change impacts on land use planning

| Category | Probability | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Macroeconomic/Political | Low | High |

**Description**

Despite its progressive policies, Rwanda has historically had limited capacity for mainstreaming climate change into government institutional practices. In many ways where the impacts of climate change impact across numerous sectors, ministries and government agencies will need to work across any perceived or real institutional barriers to align and mainstream climate change in land use planning. For example, the lack of coordination between the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (MEF) and other relevant institutions and agencies will be integral for institutionalizing the climate change adaptation processes across the Congo Nile Divide as a large interconnected landscape. Additionally, insufficient coordination, collaboration and information-sharing between these institutions and agencies may result in delays in the implementation of the Project. The lack of relevant institutions and agencies, reducing the timely delivery and effectiveness of the Project, especially the PSC, will also be an issue. Furthermore, the perception of an uneven playing field, with larger or more well-connected institutions and companies able to evade the payment of environmental fees and fines under existing legislation, may undermine the uptake of other options for financial sustainability of improved PA and forest ecosystem management.

### Mitigation Measure(s)

The Project is a part of a larger suite of efforts supported by the multi-agency Project Steering Committee (PSC) to create a spirit of cooperation among the various agencies and institutions charged with addressing climate change. The PSC will provide guidance on how to integrate climate change adaptation into regular government processes and procedures. As such, numerous government agencies have already had the opportunity to work together on a variety of climate-related issues, align institutional policies and practices, and develop strategies for mainstreaming climate change adaptation in their respective sectors. The PSC will directly oversee the Project Management Unit, and with this larger guidance structure, it is expected that the Project will be able to address unforeseen institutional or regulatory barriers encountered during the life of the Project for immediate attention and remediation. PSC will address the risk of evading the payment of environmental fees and fines under existing legislation through a task team (TTE) RSB-106/MEDC/2017 on compliance with environmental laws through greater emphasis on the links to climate resilience and NDC objectives. These measures will reduce the impact to LOW.

### Selected Risk Factor 2 - Extreme weather/climate events hinder the ability to deliver Project objectives

| Category | Probability | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Other | Low | Medium |

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V 6.0 | PAGE 124

The activities that will deliver overall Project success involve dependencies on weather conditions for successful implementation of the projects that rely on accessing steep slopes, planting trees, and establishing beekeeping operations. Extreme events such as heavy rainfall or prolonged drought could severely limit the success of these activities in the short term. These extreme events are likely to increase the risk of forest fires and decreasing the potential success of new beekeeping operations. This region, given its topography and the expected climatic variability, is likely to experience these types of disruptions. Severe disruptions may impact the project’s ability to deliver on its intended outcomes through delays in implementation or restructuring and cancellation. That said, it is unlikely these extreme conditions will present themselves in the next 5 years for the duration of the project.

## Mitigation Measure(s)

As weather is unpredictable, any mitigation measures will not change the probability nor address the impact in the short term. As the entire project is intended to increase the resiliency of this landscape to climate variability and promote adaptation, the specific activities will be able to mitigate, and in some cases prevent, longer-term impacts. As our implementation arrangements involve bolstering the climate adaptation capacity of the communities and the communities in the CDD, the entire project itself will serve as mitigation to this unlikely outcome.

## Mitigation Measure(s)

Rwanda has a successful track record of implementing large scale projects through government ministries. Competent staff will be available for project implementation, and their abilities will be enhanced through the commitment to training individuals involved in the program. The risk, if realized, may impede implementation of the Project’s activities in areas with high turnover rates and could affect GCF funding on restructuring and cancellation. Therefore, the Project will invest heavily in strengthening institutional capacity to promote climate resilience and apply actions that directly increase the resilience of ecosystems and communities. This will be achieved through a number of measures including training and mentoring to support the institutional memory to sustain Project activities in case of high staff turnover. To illustrate what may be a disproportionate distribution of benefits and burdens, although Rwanda’s population includes women and other most vulnerable people, there is a risk that the Project implementation will experience preferential treatment at the expense of these groups. This is because of Rwanda’s patriarchal culture and persistent disparities in education, employment, land ownership and other factors which gender relations in Rwanda and could cloud implementation efforts. Likewise, some vulnerable groups may be excluded from the project activities or may not have access to the resources needed for having a safe place for a new cookstove. One serious risk afflicting major projects such as that proposed, if not properly addressed, includes sexual exploitation, sexual abuse, and sexual harassment (SEAH) which may occur in the context of the Project. This could be exacerbated by the fact that women are more likely to work with women rather than men or there may be power dynamics with hired staff who work with communities and households. ## Mitigation Measure(s)

The Project anticipates these challenges and has envisioned multiple participatory aspects to the Project that are guided by the gender action plan and the ESAP. Safeguards in place to support engagement on Family Health & Safety will require training services offered at SEAH and the risk of harassment for those who engage in such activities. The Project will ensure that all project staff will be screened for prior infractions. Hired staff will be trained in survivor-centered and gender-responsive approaches, and the ESAP will include a specific section on sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA), environmental risk, the PMU and the EE will adhere to the environmental action plan and oversee the hiring of contractors to perform the activities. Multiple consultants or specialists, if part of subcontracts, will be recruited with the aim of implementing existing measures to reduce these risks. If the proposed ESAP is followed properly the impacts will be LOW.

## Description

The success of the Project depends upon the integration of activities such as beekeeping, improved cookstoves, planting of fruit trees and terrace construction on private lands by the project beneficiaries. If planned and executed incorrectly a myriad of issues could prevent beneficiaries from adopting the activities because they are not convinced that these activities will be of value to them or because they do not trust the proposed Project activities and those being implemented by other government departments or non-government organizations in the Project area.

## Mission Measure(s)

Numerous international development projects have experienced mixed results upon completion regarding the uptake of promoted activities into daily lives. This project has a strong behavior change component based on current best practices in identifying the barriers to behavior change, removing those barriers, and changing norms thus ensuring through adequate participation and training that the activities will be adopted and sustained by the beneficiaries. The Project will work closely with the communities and local government authorities (LGAs) to build long-term community ownership for the project. Further, if there are activities being promoted in other projects or programs within the same geographic region, the LGAs will be consulted on how best to integrate these activities into their own development plans.

## Mitigation Measure(s)

Since the 1990s Rwanda has set a social foundation for anti-corruption efforts by establishing policies and procedures to prevent corruption/redue vulnerability to corruption and sanctioning misbehavior through prosecution, imprisonment, or other penalties. The most recent of these is the Anti-Corruption Bill which was one proposed. The systems in place will reduce the potential for prohibited activities. Additionally, commitment to campaigns for individuals to report corruption has created a social norm for intolerance. As a result, there are no known cases of money laundering and terrorist financing in Rwanda or neighboring countries. The International Monetary Fund published an assessment of Anti Money Laundering and Combating Financing of Terrorism in 2015 indicating that while the risk of AM/LCFT is low, at this time more comprehensive measures should be taken to reduce the risk of AM/LCFT. This includes strengthening efforts to fight money laundering and terrorist financing. This was done first by enacting the law No' 091/FIC/2012 of 16th October 2012 on Financial Intelligence Center (FIC) which is responsible for monitoring, reporting, and investigating suspicious transactions in Rwanda. The government has also put in place a special agency for this purpose named Financial Intelligence Center (FIC) with a clear mission to promote financial system integrity by conducting effective financial investigations and analysis of suspicious transactions. The FIC will be responsible for the supervision on governmental institutions, projects, and parastatal agencies under the supervision of the Ministry of Finance and economic planning. MoE and the GCF Project under its supervision will also comply with FIC regulations.

The Rwanda Anti-Corruption Commission (RAC) is a body established by law to monitor and supervise the Minister General to carry out the efficiency and effectiveness of internal controls.

Regarding higher level security threats, at present, there are no known UN Security Council Sanctions against Rwanda. However, there have been sanctions on individuals in the Republic of Congo, close to the Nile Divide. The UN Security Council Consolidated Sanctions list includes approximately 20 individuals with ties to Rwanda, a small percentage of whom may live in the country. This list has been circulated to the AEIs and any potential contractors will be screened against this list.

To mitigate the risks that may occur, the MoE will maintain a Project level grievance redress mechanism to which anyone can report on the occurrence of prohibited activities. All complaints will be investigated following the process identified in Annex X. Any complaints believed to contribute to prohibited activities will be referred to the appropriate law enforcement agency.

Assuming all staff will be made aware of the prohibited activities, all subcontractors/counterparties will be screened for engagement of activities and made aware of their obligations to alert the PMU and/or submit grievances related to such activities occurring as part of the Project. The overall impact of the money laundering and terrorist financing risk on the project will be LOW.

## Selected Risk Factor 9 - Expansion of tea plantations

| Category | Probability | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Macroeconomic/Political | Low | High |

### Description
Projected climate changes project significant elevation rises in CND agro ecological zones, including the potential for tea cultivation at much higher elevations than at present. This is unlikely to threaten Rwanda's existing tea production areas, as forested mountainous regions are more likely to be affected by those from tea. However, tea remains a significant source of foreign revenue and a government target for expansion. An increased tea production in the CND would therefore most likely affect lands outside of past tea plantations. These lands will also be targets for reforestation, agroforestry, and biodiversity stepping stone initiatives under this Project.

## Mitigation Measure(s)

The integrated land use planning included in this Project design, will bring together tea industry, agriculture, forestry, biodiversity, and tourism interests to identify and reduce such potential conflicts over use of the CND's land and resource base. Through a participatory landscape-level planning we aim to establish a formal public-private sector forum at the landscape level to help improve communication across sectors, approach common land-use issues, and increase synergies between interventions to avoid conflicting targets and indicators between sectors and advocate for mainstreaming biodiversity and climate change in different economic sectors.

### G.2 Gender assessment and action plan

Women, youth and marginalized groups in the CND are key stakeholders in the Project and its primary beneficiaries. The Project will be implemented across various sectors along the CND, where natural forests are particularly vulnerable due to high population, increasing dependence upon firewood, and illegal use of timber resources. This gender analysis is based on a review of existing literature (including 10 key informant interviews) and secondary (published reports, policies and academic literature) sources to triangulate our understanding of gender in climate resilience and Project design. The Gender Analysis identifies potential barriers and opportunities for women, youth and marginalized groups along the CND.

The scoping; legislative and policy review; stakeholder consultation and analysis; and baseline analysis. The Project Officer will lead a team that includes representatives from the Ministry of Environment and Forestry, youth and gender focal points, and other relevant stakeholders to collect data on the following:

- Gender equality in climate change policies
- Gender equality in forest management policies
- Gender equality in land use policies

The Project Officer will also work with key partners such as the Women’s Empowerment Network, the Youth Council, and civil society organizations to ensure that women and youth are included in decision-making processes.

Despite tremendous policy and legal efforts, a patriarchal culture and persistent disparities characterize gender roles in Rwanda. Disparities persist across all sectors of life including education, health, employment opportunities and entrepreneurship; in decision-making at household and community levels; in family responsibilities and unpaid work care; and in the experience of violence, harassment and discrimination.

# Secretariat’s assessment of FP217

## Proposal name:
Building Resilience of Vulnerable Communities to Climate Variability in Rwanda's Congo Nile Divide through Forest and Landscape Restoration

## Accredited entity:
Ministry of Environment of Rwanda

## Country/ies:
Rwanda

## Project/programme size:
Small

### I. Overall assessment of the Secretariat

1. The funding proposal is presented to the Board for consideration with the following remarks:

#### Strengths
- This Congo Nile Divide project will safeguard Rwanda’s biodiversity, enhance climate resilience, and support vulnerable communities.
- The project is located in the Albertine Rift, which is one of the most biologically rich regions on Earth, home to 10% of Africa's birds and 49% of its mammals.

#### Points of caution
- The project would ensure linkage to other GEF funded projects in Rwanda. In addition, we encourage MOE Rwanda to establish a monitoring system that is scalable across the wider landscape.
- The Board may wish to consider funding this proposal with the terms and conditions outlined in Annexure XXI titled "List of proposed conditions and recommendations," respectively.

### II. Summary of the Secretariat’s assessment

#### 2.1 Project background
The project's goal is to improve the resilience of vulnerable communities to climate variability and shocks by increasing the extent and integrity of natural forests and by strengthening their capacity for climate-responsive forest and landscape management.


---
**Page 583**
---

### Strengthening Institutional and Regulatory Frameworks for Low-Emission Climate-Resilient Development Pathways by Mitigating Climate Change Through Integrated Land-Use Planning

#### Increase the Climate Resilience of Vulnerable Rural Communities through Forest and Landscape Restoration and Reducing Demand for Firewood

4. The proposed interventions will target districts along the Congo Nile Divide (CND) region. Rwanda's CND, an area of 446,600 hectares [1], is a high-elevation landscape of remnant forests, wetlands, and grasslands that supports diverse wildlife, including endangered farmland and commercial plantations. The CND separates the drainage basins of the Congo and Nile Rivers. It is one of the most important biodiversity hotspots in Africa and "one of the most important regions for conservation" on the continent, containing more than half of Rwanda's endemic species.

5. Though covering barely 5 percent of the country, this archipelago of protected forests is of critical importance for:

- Its globally recognized high-biodiversity values.
- Its role in Rwanda's acclaimed reforestation offerings, serving as the primary source of Rwanda's foreign revenue and as a major economic development driver.
- The ecosystem services provided for surrounding subsistence farmlands as well as commercial plantations. These include water regulation, soil conservation, and food security for women while providing the second and third highest sources of foreign revenue.
- The regulation of water capture and release to growing urban centres on the CND providing a reliable supply of water for hydroelectric power generation and other hydroelectric operations; and
- The sequestration and storage of nearly 50 percent of Rwanda's national carbon stocks.

6. These ecosystem services are already compromised by a combination of anthropogenic and climatic factors; they will be much more severely threatened by the potential negative feedbacks from climate change. The proposed project will implement an ecosystem-based approach to forest protection and restoration and will increase the extent and resilience of forests, trees, and species, including those currently isolated forest fragments. Through this approach, the project will protect, restore, and rehabilitate forest ecosystems, thus enhancing biodiversity and reducing key threats while increasing the provision of ecosystem services.

7. Project interventions will directly benefit 1,254,242 people (654,404 women). The project will also indirectly benefit 9,283,745 people and create approximately 24,212 job opportunities in the CND region. The project is estimated to sequester an amount equivalent to 1,204,488 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂ eq) by 2043.

8. The project will be implemented with a total budget of USD 59,056,422. The Rwanda Forests Authority (RFA), Rwanda Water Board (RWB), Rwanda Development Board (RDB) and the Ministry of Environment of Rwanda (MoE Rwanda) will provide technical support to the project. The project is eligible for co-financing in kind contribution of USD 122,278. The project is submitted under environmental and social safeguards (ESS) category B.


---
**Page 584**
---

2. **Component-by-component analysis**

   **Component 1: Mainstreaming climate adaptation into integrated land-use planning (total cost: USD 9.2 million; GCF cost: USD 2.3 million)**

      - This component aims to mainstream climate change adaptation considerations into land-use planning at the national and subnational levels.
      The goal is to achieve climate resilience through the integration of climate information in land-use plans, with support from development partners.
      The component has two main outputs:
         * Output 1: To develop a climate-resilient land-use plan for the CBO by integrating climate adaptation information into existing land-use planning processes. This will enhance the adaptive capacity and resilience of natural ecosystems to integrate biodiversity and climate risks into land-use plans.

   **Component 2: Climate change management and restoration (total cost: USD 18.9 million; GCF cost: USD 16.3 million)**

      - In this component, targeted interventions will increase climate change awareness and adaptation capacity in rural communities.
      The activities will focus on restoring degraded areas within those parks.
      These efforts will help sustain the forests' rich biodiversity, improve ecosystem services, and provide essential environmental services needed for the climate resilience of vulnerable communities.
      The suite of activities will also identify priority areas outside of parks – in remnant natural stands, around wetlands and along riverbanks.

   **Component 3: Enhancing climate adaptation through resilient livelihoods (total cost: USD 22.6 million; GCF cost: USD 17.2 million)**

      - The activities under this component aim to combine environmental conservation with socioeconomic development.
      Creating a multifaceted approach that resonates with the global conservation agenda and contributes to poverty alleviation by conserving forest plantations, providing sustainable fuel sources, delivering carbon sequestration benefits totaling $24,000 per CO2 tonne, and generating additional income.
      The other activities focus on rural livelihoods, financial services, and sustainable food production methods.

      - The component will support reforestation on steep slopes on both public and smallholder farms. This will be done by planting trees that produce timber and/or non-timber forest products such as fruits, nuts, and medicinal species.
      These will produce firewood and/or market products, while conserving and enriching soils.
      The component will also support the production of agroforestry systems or alternative value chain products that provide both natural services, including soil conservation, water retention, income generation, beekeeping, and improved cooking stoves. 
      Central to these activities will be the facilitation of access to markets for farmers, traders, processors, and maintaining businesses.
      Given that these activities are designed at the core to be profitable and sustainable independently, it is expected to be replicable and sustained once GCF funding expires.
